Kernel.title: Kernel — Ramos
Kernel.heading: Kernel
Kernel.body:
Summary

Kernel — the implicit, always-in-scope module of built-ins.

Module documentation

Kernel — the implicit, always-in-scope module of built-ins.

Kernel is auto-imported into every scope, so its functions are the only ones you call bare — print(x) is sugar for Kernel.print(x), and no alias is ever needed for it. Every other module must be named or aliased.

It is the seam between Ramos code and the host runtime. Its functions have no Ramos bodies: each delegates to a native handler via native(str, args), which the interpreter intercepts and dispatches. As a result Kernel collects the primitives that can't reasonably be expressed in Ramos itself:

  • console I/O — print, println, new_line, read, read_all, read_password, eprint, eprintln
  • process — get_args, get_arg, get_env, sleep, exit
  • time — now (wall clock), monotonic (elapsed)
  • randomness — random, random_int (not cryptographic)
  • collection ops — size (List/Tuple/Map), at (List/Tuple), to_list, is_empty (also strings)
  • conversions — to_string (display), inspect (debug), to_integer, to_float, type_of (there is deliberately no to_symbol — see below)
  • calling — apply(f, args), module_apply(m, fn_name, args) (see the Module module)
  • control flow — loop(f) (pure Ramos, no native — Ramos has no while/for, so this is the one way to repeat something an unknown number of times)
  • actors — start_actor, call_actor, cast_actor, list_actors, actor_stats, is_actor_started, stop_actor
  • diagnostics — current_stacktrace
  • errors — error(type, message) (with a stacktrace) and exception(type, message) (without, for business logic) — see "Error handling" in the README
  • type predicates — is_integer, is_string, is_list, …
  • truthiness — is_truthy (pure Ramos, no native; not inverts it)

Because Kernel is always in scope, these read as language-level built-ins rather than library calls:

print("hi")
n = size([1, 2, 3])
cond
  is_tuple(value) -> ...

Conventions:

  • out-of-range at returns nil.
  • the is_* predicates mirror the built-in type modules listed in the README's Types table (plus is_lambda for anonymous functions).
  • there is no to_symbol, by design. A symbol lives for as long as the program does, so building one from runtime data — a request field, a line of input — is an unbounded leak. Symbols are written as literals (:ok), which keeps the set of them finite and visible in the source. To carry runtime text, use a String; to branch on it, match the string and yield a literal symbol.

Functions

function native(str, args) Invokes a host-provided (native) function by name.
function print(value) Writes value to standard out without a trailing newline, then flushes. value is rendered with its String representation.
function println(value) Writes value to standard out followed by a newline. Like print(value); new_line(), but the text and its newline are written in a single call, so when threads print at once one line never lands inside another (see the Thread module).
function new_line() Writes a single newline (\n) to standard out and flushes. Useful for terminating a sequence of print calls.
function read() Reads a single line from standard in (up to and including the newline, which is stripped) and returns it as a String. Blocks until a line is available; returns nil at end-of-input.
function read_password() Reads a line from standard in without echoing it to the terminal, and returns it as a String. Intended for secrets like passwords. Returns nil at end-of-input. Behavior falls back to plain echoing read when the input stream is not a TTY.
function read_all() Reads all of standard in, to end of input, as a single String — the whole-pipe counterpart to read, which takes one line. Returns "" when the input is empty.
function eprint(value) Writes value to standard error without a trailing newline. Use it for diagnostics, so a program's real output on standard out stays clean enough to pipe.
function eprintln(value) eprint with a trailing newline.
function get_env(name) Looks up an environment variable by name and returns its String value, or nil if it is not set.
function get_args() Returns the program's command-line arguments — everything after the script path — as a List of Strings. Empty when none were given.
function get_arg(index) Returns the command-line argument at zero-based index, or nil if there is no argument at that position. Negative indexes are not supported.
function sleep(ms) Suspends the program for ms milliseconds, then returns nil. A value of 0 or less returns immediately.
function exit(code) Ends the program with code as its exit status — 0 for success, any other value for failure. Nothing after the call runs.
function now() The wall-clock time as milliseconds since the Unix epoch.
function monotonic() Milliseconds from a fixed point in the program's life. The value only ever moves forward, which is what makes it the right clock for measuring how long something took.
function random() A random Float in [0.0, 1.0) — zero is possible, one is not.
function random_int(low, high) A random Integer in low..high, inclusive at both ends. The bounds may be given either way round.
function apply(f, args) Calls the lambda f with args, a list of its arguments. Use it when the arity is not known where the call is written — otherwise call f directly.
function module_apply(m, fn_name, args) Resolves fn_name on module m and calls it with args, a list. Module.apply is the client-side name for this — prefer it.
function loop(f) Calls f, a lambda of no arguments, over and over — for its side effects, since nothing is threaded between calls — until it returns the symbol :halt. This is Ramos's while(true): there is no while or for, so loop is the one way to repeat something an unknown number of times, such as a server's accept loop:
function start_actor(id, actor_module, initial_state, config) Starts an actor under id, handled by module — which must implement the Actor trait — holding initial_state. config is fixed for the actor's lifetime and passed to every call and cast.
function call_actor(id, actor_module, op, args) Sends op to the actor registered under id and waits for the reply. The module's call(f, args, state, config) handles it and returns a (reply, new_state) tuple: the reply comes back here, and new_state is what the actor holds from then on.
function cast_actor(id, actor_module, op, args) Sends op to the actor registered under id without waiting for it to be handled, and returns :ok at once. The message goes on the actor's mailbox and runs later: before the next call_actor on that actor, or when the program ends, whichever comes first.
function list_actors() Every running actor as an (id, module) pair, sorted by id so the order is stable from one call to the next. The id is the value it was started with, and the module is the module itself — so a pair can be handed straight to call_actor or cast_actor.
function actor_stats(id) What is known about one running actor, as a Map:
function is_actor_started(id) Whether id names a running actor. False for an id that was never started, and for one that has been stopped.
function stop_actor(id) Lets the actor finish everything already sent to it, then ends its thread and forgets the id. Nothing in flight is discarded: the stop is queued behind the messages already in the mailbox.
function size(collection) Returns the number of elements in collection — the length of a List, the arity of a Tuple, or the number of key/value pairs in a Map. Strings are not collections: size on a String is an error — use String.length instead.
function at(collection, index) Returns the element of collection at zero-based index (List or Tuple), or nil if out of range. Negative indexes are not supported. Strings are not collections: at on a String is an error — use String.at instead.
function to_string(value) Converts value to its String representation — the same rendering that print uses. Numbers, symbols, tuples, lists, and maps all stringify; nil becomes "nil".
function to_integer(value) Converts value to an Integer. A String is parsed as a whole number; a Float is truncated toward zero. Returns nil if value can't be parsed.
function to_float(value) Converts value to a Float. An Integer widens; a String is parsed as a decimal number. Returns nil if value can't be parsed.
function to_list(value) Converts value to a List. A Tuple yields its elements in order; a Map yields its values (keys are dropped — reach for the Map module when you need them). Already-list values are returned unchanged.
function current_stacktrace() Returns the current call stacktrace — the chain of Ramos calls leading to this point — as a list of (file, line) tuples, most recent call first and the outermost caller (main, or wherever the trail runs out) last.
function error(type, message) Builds the standard error tuple: (:error, (type, message, stacktrace)). This — together with exception, its stackless twin — is the one way Ramos code reports failure: there is no raise and no catch. A fallible function returns (:ok, value) on success and whatever this builds on failure, and the caller reads either with case like any other value.
function exception(type, message) Builds the business-logic error tuple: (:error, (type, message)) — the same shape as error, minus the stacktrace.
function is_integer(value) Returns true if value is an Integer.
function is_float(value) Returns true if value is a Float.
function is_string(value) Returns true if value is a String.
function is_symbol(value) Returns true if value is a Symbol (e.g. :ok).
function is_bool(value) Returns true if value is a Bool (true or false).
function is_nil(value) Returns true if value is nil.
function is_list(value) Returns true if value is a List.
function is_tuple(value) Returns true if value is a Tuple.
function is_map(value) Returns true if value is a Map.
function is_module(value) Returns true if value is a Module.
function is_struct(value) Returns true if value is a Struct instance.
function inspect(value) The debug rendering of value: strings keep their quotes and symbols their colon, so a value reads back as the source that would build it. This is what the REPL prints and what error messages quote.
function type_of(value) The module value belongs to — the one the README's Types table lists.
function is_empty(value) Whether value holds nothing — an empty list, map, tuple or string.
function is_truthy(value) Whether value counts as true in a condition. Only false and nil are falsy — every other value, including 0, "" and [], is truthy. This is the rule if, cond, and, or and not all use.
function is_lambda(value) Returns true if value is a Lambda (an anonymous function).

function native(str, args) ¶

Invokes a host-provided (native) function by name.

str is the name of the native function to call, and args is a list of arguments to forward to it. This function has no Ramos body — the interpreter intercepts the call and dispatches it to the corresponding native handler in the host runtime.

native("print", ["hello"])   # handled by the interpreter
str
the name of the native handler to invoke
args
a List of arguments forwarded to the handler

Returns: whatever the native handler returns

function print(value) ¶

Writes value to standard out without a trailing newline, then flushes. value is rendered with its String representation.

print("loading")        # -> loading
value
the value to write (rendered as a String)

Returns: nil

function println(value) ¶

Writes value to standard out followed by a newline. Like print(value); new_line(), but the text and its newline are written in a single call, so when threads print at once one line never lands inside another (see the Thread module).

println("done")         # -> done\n
value
the value to write (rendered as a String)

Returns: nil

function new_line() ¶

Writes a single newline (\n) to standard out and flushes. Useful for terminating a sequence of print calls.

print("a")
print("b")
new_line()             # -> ab\n

Returns: nil

function read() ¶

Reads a single line from standard in (up to and including the newline, which is stripped) and returns it as a String. Blocks until a line is available; returns nil at end-of-input.

name = read()

Returns: the line read as a String, or nil at end-of-input

function read_password() ¶

Reads a line from standard in without echoing it to the terminal, and returns it as a String. Intended for secrets like passwords. Returns nil at end-of-input. Behavior falls back to plain echoing read when the input stream is not a TTY.

pw = read_password()

Returns: the line read as a String, or nil at end-of-input

function read_all() ¶

Reads all of standard in, to end of input, as a single String — the whole-pipe counterpart to read, which takes one line. Returns "" when the input is empty.

text = read_all()      # `cat file | ramos run app.rmo`

Returns: everything on standard in as a String

function eprint(value) ¶

Writes value to standard error without a trailing newline. Use it for diagnostics, so a program's real output on standard out stays clean enough to pipe.

Unlike print, standard error is never buffered — a message is on screen as soon as it is written.

eprint("warning: ")
value
the value to write

Returns: nil

function eprintln(value) ¶

eprint with a trailing newline.

eprintln("could not read config, using defaults")
value
the value to write

Returns: nil

function get_env(name) ¶

Looks up an environment variable by name and returns its String value, or nil if it is not set.

get_env("HOME")        # == "/home/andrew"
name
the environment variable name to look up

Returns: the variable's String value, or nil if unset

function get_args() ¶

Returns the program's command-line arguments — everything after the script path — as a List of Strings. Empty when none were given.

# ramos run app.rmo alice 42
get_args()             # == ["alice", "42"]

Returns: a List of the argument Strings (empty when none were given)

function get_arg(index) ¶

Returns the command-line argument at zero-based index, or nil if there is no argument at that position. Negative indexes are not supported.

# ramos run app.rmo alice 42
get_arg(0)             # == "alice"
get_arg(9)             # == nil
index
the zero-based position of the argument to read

Returns: the argument String at index, or nil if there is none

function sleep(ms) ¶

Suspends the program for ms milliseconds, then returns nil. A value of 0 or less returns immediately.

sleep(250)             # pause for a quarter second
ms
how many milliseconds to sleep (0 or less returns at once)

Returns: nil

function exit(code) ¶

Ends the program with code as its exit status — 0 for success, any other value for failure. Nothing after the call runs.

Output written with print is flushed on the way out, so a program can print its result and exit in the next breath without losing it.

exit(0)                # success
exit(1)                # failure
code
the process exit status

Returns: never returns

function now() ¶

The wall-clock time as milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

This is the clock to timestamp with. It can jump backwards when the system clock is adjusted, so measure elapsed time with monotonic.

started = now()

Returns: an Integer — milliseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC

function monotonic() ¶

Milliseconds from a fixed point in the program's life. The value only ever moves forward, which is what makes it the right clock for measuring how long something took.

The origin is arbitrary, so a single reading means nothing on its own — only the difference between two does.

started = monotonic()
# ... work ...
elapsed = monotonic() - started

Returns: an Integer — milliseconds since an arbitrary fixed point

function random() ¶

A random Float in [0.0, 1.0) — zero is possible, one is not.

Not cryptographic: this is for sampling, shuffling and test data, never for secrets or tokens.

chance = random()

Returns: a Float in [0.0, 1.0)

function random_int(low, high) ¶

A random Integer in low..high, inclusive at both ends. The bounds may be given either way round.

Not cryptographic — see random.

roll = random_int(1, 6)
low
one end of the range
high
the other end of the range

Returns: an Integer between the two, inclusive

function apply(f, args) ¶

Calls the lambda f with args, a list of its arguments. Use it when the arity is not known where the call is written — otherwise call f directly.

Like native, this function has no Ramos body: the interpreter intercepts the call, because running a lambda needs the evaluator and a native handler cannot reach back into it. Also like native, it is answered for the bare call apply(...), not for Kernel.apply(...).

apply(do x, y -> x + y, [1, 2])   # == 3
apply(do -> 42, [])               # == 42
f
the lambda to call
args
a List of the arguments to pass

Returns: whatever f returns

function module_apply(m, fn_name, args) ¶

Resolves fn_name on module m and calls it with args, a list. Module.apply is the client-side name for this — prefer it.

Enforces the same helper visibility a written m.fn_name(...) call would: a private function is reachable only from inside its own module, so this cannot reach around that rule from the outside.

Like apply, this function has no Ramos body: the interpreter intercepts the call, since resolving fn_name and running it needs the evaluator. Also like apply, it is answered for the bare call module_apply(...), not for Kernel.module_apply(...).

module_apply(Integer, "abs", [-7])   # == 7
m
the module to call a function on
fn_name
the function's name, as a String
args
a List of the arguments to pass

Returns: whatever the resolved function returns

function loop(f) ¶

Calls f, a lambda of no arguments, over and over — for its side effects, since nothing is threaded between calls — until it returns the symbol :halt. This is Ramos's while(true): there is no while or for, so loop is the one way to repeat something an unknown number of times, such as a server's accept loop:

accept_loop =
  do
    case ServerSocket.accept(server)
      (:ok, conn) -> handle(conn)
      (:error, reason) -> println("accept failed: #{reason}")
    :continue
loop(accept_loop)

This has no Rust loop underneath it and needs none. loop is an ordinary Ramos function whose last expression is a self-recursive tail call (loop(f) again), and the interpreter trampolines exactly that shape into a plain loop on its own side — the same mechanism List.each and every other tail-recursive stdlib function already leans on. Each pass calls f(), matches its result, and either stops or re-enters loop in place — the call frame is reused rather than growing, so the native stack stays flat no matter how many times it runs. A loop meant to run for the life of the program (a server's accept loop, an event pump) is exactly what this is for.

What is not free: f itself still runs on the native stack for the duration of one call, same as any function call, so a call inside f that never returns (a blocking read with nothing on the other end, an unbounded recursion of its own) blocks loop right there — loop cannot see or interrupt it. And a failure f does not catch — a pattern match with no matching arm, a native error — stops the whole loop (and, uncaught, the program) at that call, exactly as any other runtime error would; wrap risky work in a case inside f rather than relying on loop to survive it.

Global.start()
Global.put(:count, 0)
step =
  do
    n = Global.get(:count) + 1
    Global.put(:count, n)
    case n
      3 -> :halt
      _ -> :continue
loop(step)
Global.get(:count)   # == 3
f
a lambda of no arguments, called repeatedly for its effect

Returns: :halt

function start_actor(id, actor_module, initial_state, config) ¶

Starts an actor under id, handled by module — which must implement the Actor trait — holding initial_state. config is fixed for the actor's lifetime and passed to every call and cast.

The id is what identifies a running actor, so one module can back many of them, each with its own state. Starting the same id twice is an error.

Like apply, this function has no Ramos body: the interpreter intercepts the call, because dispatching a message runs Ramos code and a native handler cannot reach back into the evaluator. Also like apply, it is answered for the bare call start_actor(...), not Kernel.start_actor(...).

start_actor(:global, Global, {}, {})
id
the name to register the actor under, conventionally a symbol
actor_module
the module implementing Actor
initial_state
the state the actor starts with
config
fixed configuration handed to every callback

Returns: :ok

function call_actor(id, actor_module, op, args) ¶

Sends op to the actor registered under id and waits for the reply. The module's call(f, args, state, config) handles it and returns a (reply, new_state) tuple: the reply comes back here, and new_state is what the actor holds from then on.

Any messages sent earlier with cast_actor are handled first, in the order they were sent, so a call always sees everything sent before it.

Has no Ramos body, for the reason given on start_actor.

call_actor(:global, Global, :get, ["key"])
id
the actor's id, as given to start_actor
actor_module
the module handling that actor
op
the operation, conventionally a symbol such as :get
args
a List of arguments for the operation

Returns: whatever the handler put in the reply position

function cast_actor(id, actor_module, op, args) ¶

Sends op to the actor registered under id without waiting for it to be handled, and returns :ok at once. The message goes on the actor's mailbox and runs later: before the next call_actor on that actor, or when the program ends, whichever comes first.

The module's cast(f, args, state, config) handles it and returns only the new state — a cast has no reply to send anywhere. Unless the module defines its own, the Actor trait's default runs call and discards the reply.

Because the handler runs later, a failure inside it surfaces later too: at the drain, after the statement that sent the message.

Has no Ramos body, for the reason given on start_actor.

cast_actor(:global, Global, :clear, ["key"])
id
the actor's id, as given to start_actor
actor_module
the module handling that actor
op
the operation, conventionally a symbol
args
a List of arguments for the operation

Returns: :ok, immediately

function list_actors() ¶

Every running actor as an (id, module) pair, sorted by id so the order is stable from one call to the next. The id is the value it was started with, and the module is the module itself — so a pair can be handed straight to call_actor or cast_actor.

Has no Ramos body, for the reason given on start_actor.

list_actors()   # == []
[(id, mod) | _] = list_actors()
call_actor(id, mod, :ping, [])

Returns: a List of (id, module) tuples

function actor_stats(id) ¶

What is known about one running actor, as a Map:

  • id — the id it was started with
  • module — the name of the module handling it, as a String
  • calls — how many call_actor messages have been sent to it
  • casts — how many cast_actor messages have been sent to it
  • pending — casts sent whose outcome has not been collected yet
  • alive — whether its thread is still running

calls and casts count messages sent. A cast is asynchronous, so it may still be running: pending is the part not accounted for yet, and drops to zero once the handler has finished and its result been collected.

Has no Ramos body, for the reason given on start_actor.

actor_stats(:global)
id
the actor's id, as given to start_actor

Returns: a Map describing the actor

function is_actor_started(id) ¶

Whether id names a running actor. False for an id that was never started, and for one that has been stopped.

Has no Ramos body, for the reason given on start_actor.

is_actor_started(:nobody)   # == false
id
the id to test

Returns: true when an actor is running under id

function stop_actor(id) ¶

Lets the actor finish everything already sent to it, then ends its thread and forgets the id. Nothing in flight is discarded: the stop is queued behind the messages already in the mailbox.

Afterwards the id is free, so start_actor may reuse it. Sending to a stopped actor is an error, the same as sending to one never started.

Has no Ramos body, for the reason given on start_actor.

stop_actor(:global)
id
the actor's id, as given to start_actor

Returns: :ok

function size(collection) ¶

Returns the number of elements in collection — the length of a List, the arity of a Tuple, or the number of key/value pairs in a Map. Strings are not collections: size on a String is an error — use String.length instead.

size([1, 2, 3])            # == 3
size((:ok, 42))            # == 2
size({a: 1, b: 2})         # == 2
collection
a List, Tuple, or Map

Returns: the Integer element count

function at(collection, index) ¶

Returns the element of collection at zero-based index (List or Tuple), or nil if out of range. Negative indexes are not supported. Strings are not collections: at on a String is an error — use String.at instead.

at([1, 2, 3], 1)      # == 2
at((:ok, 42), 1)      # == 42
at([1, 2, 3], 9)      # == nil
collection
a List or Tuple
index
the zero-based position to read

Returns: the element at index, or nil if out of range

function to_string(value) ¶

Converts value to its String representation — the same rendering that print uses. Numbers, symbols, tuples, lists, and maps all stringify; nil becomes "nil".

to_string(42)          # == "42"
to_string(:ok)         # == ":ok"
value
the value to render

Returns: the String representation of value

function to_integer(value) ¶

Converts value to an Integer. A String is parsed as a whole number; a Float is truncated toward zero. Returns nil if value can't be parsed.

to_integer("42")     # == 42
to_integer(3.9)      # == 3
value
a String, Float, or Integer to convert

Returns: the Integer value, or nil if it can't be parsed

function to_float(value) ¶

Converts value to a Float. An Integer widens; a String is parsed as a decimal number. Returns nil if value can't be parsed.

to_float(3)          # == 3.0
to_float("3.14")     # == 3.14
value
an Integer, String, or Float to convert

Returns: the Float value, or nil if it can't be parsed

function to_list(value) ¶

Converts value to a List. A Tuple yields its elements in order; a Map yields its values (keys are dropped — reach for the Map module when you need them). Already-list values are returned unchanged.

to_list((1, 2, 3))         # == [1, 2, 3]
to_list({a: 1, b: 2})      # == [1, 2]
value
a Tuple, Map, or List

Returns: a List — a tuple's elements, a map's values, or the list itself

function current_stacktrace() ¶

Returns the current call stacktrace — the chain of Ramos calls leading to this point — as a list of (file, line) tuples, most recent call first and the outermost caller (main, or wherever the trail runs out) last.

A self-recursive tail call is not a frame of its own: it loops in constant space rather than recursing, so however many times it has looped, it still contributes exactly one entry — the line the loop is currently at.

print(current_stacktrace())

Returns: a List of (file, line) tuples, most recent call first

function error(type, message) ¶

Builds the standard error tuple: (:error, (type, message, stacktrace)). This — together with exception, its stackless twin — is the one way Ramos code reports failure: there is no raise and no catch. A fallible function returns (:ok, value) on success and whatever this builds on failure, and the caller reads either with case like any other value.

type is a lowercase symbol naming what went wrong — the part code matches on. message is for the human reading the output: a String, or a struct when a plain string is not enough detail. The stacktrace is current_stacktrace(), captured where error is called, so a failure carries where it came from without a caller having to ask for it.

Reach for error where that trace earns its cost — a lower-level or unexpected failure worth tracing back. Ordinary business-rule failures (a bad request, a declined charge) happen too often and too predictably for a trace to be useful — use exception for those.

built = error(:insufficient_funds, "balance is too low")
(:error, (type, message, _)) = built
(type, message)   # == (:insufficient_funds, "balance is too low")
type
a symbol naming what went wrong
message
a String, or a struct carrying further detail

Returns: (:error, (type, message, stacktrace))

function exception(type, message) ¶

Builds the business-logic error tuple: (:error, (type, message)) — the same shape as error, minus the stacktrace.

An expected failure — a bad request, a declined charge, a value that fails validation — happens in the ordinary run of a program and is handled a line or two away, so a stacktrace would only be noise. Use exception for those, and save error (which captures one) for a failure worth tracing back to where it happened.

exception(:insufficient_funds, "balance is too low")
# == (:error, (:insufficient_funds, "balance is too low"))
type
a symbol naming what went wrong
message
a String, or a struct carrying further detail

Returns: (:error, (type, message))

function is_integer(value) ¶

Returns true if value is an Integer.

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is an Integer, else false

function is_float(value) ¶

Returns true if value is a Float.

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a Float, else false

function is_string(value) ¶

Returns true if value is a String.

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a String, else false

function is_symbol(value) ¶

Returns true if value is a Symbol (e.g. :ok).

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a Symbol, else false

function is_bool(value) ¶

Returns true if value is a Bool (true or false).

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a Bool, else false

function is_nil(value) ¶

Returns true if value is nil.

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is nil, else false

function is_list(value) ¶

Returns true if value is a List.

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a List, else false

the value to test

Returns true if value is a Map.

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a Map, else false

Returns true if value is a Module.

the value to test

Returns true if value is a Struct instance.

function inspect(value) ¶

The debug rendering of value: strings keep their quotes and symbols their colon, so a value reads back as the source that would build it. This is what the REPL prints and what error messages quote.

to_string gives the display form instead, which renders a string bare. The two differ only at the top level — a string nested inside a list is quoted either way.

inspect("hi")        # == "\"hi\""
to_string("hi")      # == "hi"
inspect([1, "two"])  # == "[1, \"two\"]"
inspect(:ok)         # == ":ok"
value
the value to render

Returns: a String — the debug rendering

function type_of(value) ¶

The module value belongs to — the one the README's Types table lists.

A String rather than a Symbol: module names are CamelCase and symbol names are snake_case, so :Integer is not a symbol you could write, and a value you cannot write is a poor thing to compare against.

type_of(42)        # == "Integer"
type_of(3.14)      # == "Float"
type_of("hi")      # == "String"
type_of([1, 2])    # == "List"
type_of(nil)       # == "Nil"

function is_empty(value) ¶

Whether value holds nothing — an empty list, map, tuple or string.

is_empty({})       # == true
is_empty("")       # == true
is_empty([1])      # == false
is_empty("hi")     # == false
value
a list, map, tuple or string

Returns: true when it holds no elements or characters

function is_truthy(value) ¶

Whether value counts as true in a condition. Only false and nil are falsy — every other value, including 0, "" and [], is truthy. This is the rule if, cond, and, or and not all use.

There is no native behind this one: a cond arm already tests a value for truthiness, so the function is that rule written down.

is_truthy(0)       # == true
is_truthy("")      # == true
is_truthy([])      # == true
is_truthy(nil)     # == false
is_truthy(false)   # == false
value
the value to test

Returns: true when value is truthy, false when it is false or nil

Returns true if value is a Lambda (an anonymous function).

value
the value to test

Returns: true if value is a Lambda, else false

Summary

Integer — operations on whole numbers.

Module documentation

Integer — operations on whole numbers.

42 is an Integer. Arithmetic lives in the operators (+, -, *, /, %, **) rather than here; this module holds what reads better as a named function, especially the predicates passed to List:

[1, 2, 3, 4]
| List.filter(do x -> Integer.is_even(x))   # == [2, 4]

Kernel already converts, so this module does not repeat it: use to_integer(text) to parse, to_float(n) to widen, to_string(n) to render.

Conventions:

  • integer division truncates toward zero, and % follows the sign of the divisor — both are operator behaviour, documented in the README.

Float.title: Float — Ramos
Float.heading: Float
Float.body:
Summary

Float — operations on floating-point numbers.

Module documentation

Float — operations on floating-point numbers.

3.14 is a Float. Arithmetic lives in the operators (+, -, *, /, **); this module holds the rounding, the constants, and the tests that read better as named functions.

Float.round(2.6)   # == 3
Float.pi()         # == 3.141592653589793

An Integer and a Float never compare equal — 1 == 1.0 is false — so convert explicitly when you mean to compare across the two.

Rounding is built on Kernel's to_integer (which truncates toward zero), and the special values fall out of the arithmetic itself — no native needed for either. exp/log/log_two/log_ten/sin/cos/tan are the exception: transcendental functions have no operator to build on, so those seven are the only natives behind this module. (No digit may appear in a Ramos identifier, which is why the base-2 and base-10 logs are spelled out rather than log2/log10.)

Kernel already converts and truncates, so this module does not repeat it: use to_integer(x) to drop the fraction, to_float(text) to parse, and to_string(x) to render.

Conventions:

  • floor, ceil and round all return an Integer.
  • round goes half away from zero: 2.5 rounds to 3, -2.5 to -3.

Functions

function pi() The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
function e() Euler's number, the base of the natural logarithm.
function infinity() Positive infinity. Negate it for the other end: -Float.infinity().
function nan() Not-a-number, the result of an undefined operation. It equals nothing, including itself, so test it with is_nan rather than ==.
function floor(x) The largest integer not greater than x.
function ceil(x) The smallest integer not less than x.
function round(x) x rounded to the nearest integer, halves going away from zero.
function abs(x) The magnitude of x, without its sign.
function sqrt(x) The square root of x, via x ** 0.5. A negative x yields nan.
function min(a, b) The smaller of two floats.
function max(a, b) The larger of two floats.
function clamp(x, low, high) x held inside the range low..high.
function compare(a, b) Orders two floats as -1, 0 or 1 — the shape sorting wants.
function is_nan(x) Whether x is the not-a-number value. nan is the one value not equal to itself, which is exactly how this is tested.
function is_infinite(x) Whether x is positive or negative infinity.
function is_finite(x) Whether x is an ordinary number — neither infinite nor nan.
function sign(x) -1.0, 0.0 or 1.0 according to the sign of x. Neither infinity nor nan gets special treatment: sign on an infinity follows its direction, same as any other float, and nan < 0.0/nan > 0.0 are both false so sign(Float.nan()) is 0.0 — the same convention compare already uses for nan.
function is_positive(x) Whether x is strictly greater than zero.
function is_negative(x) Whether x is strictly less than zero.
function exp(x) Euler's number e raised to the power x. The one direction ** cannot express directly, since the base there is the fixed operand.
function log(x) The natural logarithm of x (base e) — the inverse of exp. Negative x yields nan; 0.0 yields -Float.infinity().
function log_two(x) The base-2 logarithm of x. Same domain as log.
function log_ten(x) The base-10 logarithm of x. Same domain as log.
function sin(x) The sine of x, in radians.
function cos(x) The cosine of x, in radians.
function tan(x) The tangent of x, in radians.

String.title: String — Ramos
String.heading: String
String.body:
Summary

String — operations on immutable, UTF-8 text.

Module documentation

String — operations on immutable, UTF-8 text.

Strings in Ramos are double-quoted ("hi"), interpolated with #{name}, and concatenated with <>. Like every value in Ramos they are immutable: every function here returns a new string rather than mutating its input.

Unlike lists, strings have no head | tail destructuring in the language, so the character-level primitives (indexing, slicing, casing, splitting, reversing) delegate to the host via native. Concatenation is the <> operator rather than a function here, and the rest compose through pipes just like the List module:

"  Hello World  "
| String.trim()
| String.downcase()
| String.replace(" ", "_")     # == "hello_world"

Joining a list of strings back into one is List.join (not here), the natural inverse of split. Numeric parsing lives on Kernel (to_integer / to_float), and so does emptiness: is_empty(s) already covers strings, so this module does not repeat it.

Conventions:

  • indexes are zero-based and count Unicode code points.
  • at returns a single-character string; Ramos has no separate char type.
  • search functions that may miss return nil.

Functions

function length(s) Returns the number of Unicode code points in s.
function at(s, index) Returns the single-character string at zero-based index, or nil if out of range. Ramos has no separate char type, so the result is a String.
function slice(s, start, count) Returns count characters of s starting at zero-based start. start beyond the end yields ""; count is clipped to the available tail.
function contains(s, sub) Returns true if sub occurs anywhere within s, else false.
function starts_with(s, prefix) Returns true if s begins with prefix, else false.
function ends_with(s, suffix) Returns true if s ends with suffix, else false.
function find(s, sub) Returns the zero-based index of the first occurrence of sub in s, or nil if it is not present.
function replace(s, pattern, replacement) Returns a copy of s with every (non-overlapping) occurrence of pattern replaced by replacement.
function split(s, sep) Splits s at each occurrence of sep, returning a list of parts. Empty sep splits into one-character strings. To rejoin, use List.join.
function upcase(s) Returns s with each ASCII letter uppercased.
function downcase(s) Returns s with each ASCII letter lowercased.
function trim(s) Returns s with leading and trailing whitespace removed.
function trim_left(s) Returns s with leading whitespace removed.
function trim_right(s) Returns s with trailing whitespace removed.
function reverse(s) Returns s with its characters in reverse order.
function repeat(s, n) Returns s concatenated with itself n times. n <= 0 yields "".
function to_list(s) Splits s into a list of single-character strings, one per Unicode code point. The inverse of from_list.
function pad_left(s, width, pad_char) Returns s left-padded with pad_char until it reaches at least width characters. Already-long-enough s comes back unchanged. pad_char is a single character; a longer one may overshoot width.
function pad_right(s, width, pad_char) Returns s right-padded with pad_char until it reaches at least width characters. Already-long-enough s comes back unchanged. pad_char is a single character; a longer one may overshoot width.
function capitalize(s) Returns s with its first character uppercased and the rest lowercased. "" comes back unchanged.
function from_list(chars) Concatenates a list of single-character strings into one string. The inverse of to_list.

function length(s) ¶

Returns the number of Unicode code points in s.

String.length("hello")   # == 5
s
the string to measure

Returns: the Integer count of code points in s

function at(s, index) ¶

Returns the single-character string at zero-based index, or nil if out of range. Ramos has no separate char type, so the result is a String.

String.at("hello", 1)   # == "e"
String.at("hello", 9)   # == nil
s
the string to read from
index
the zero-based code-point position to read

Returns: the single-character String at index, or nil if out of range

function slice(s, start, count) ¶

Returns count characters of s starting at zero-based start. start beyond the end yields ""; count is clipped to the available tail.

String.slice("hello world", 0, 5)   # == "hello"
s
the string to slice
start
the zero-based code-point position to start at
count
how many characters to take

Returns: a new String of up to count characters from start

function contains(s, sub) ¶

Returns true if sub occurs anywhere within s, else false.

String.contains("hello world", "world")   # == true
s
the string to search within
sub
the substring to look for

Returns: true if sub occurs in s, else false

function starts_with(s, prefix) ¶

Returns true if s begins with prefix, else false.

String.starts_with("hello", "he")   # == true
s
the string to test
prefix
the prefix to look for

Returns: true if s begins with prefix, else false

function ends_with(s, suffix) ¶

Returns true if s ends with suffix, else false.

String.ends_with("hello", "lo")   # == true
s
the string to test
suffix
the suffix to look for

Returns: true if s ends with suffix, else false

function find(s, sub) ¶

Returns the zero-based index of the first occurrence of sub in s, or nil if it is not present.

String.find("hello world", "world")   # == 6
String.find("hello", "z")             # == nil
s
the string to search within
sub
the substring to look for

Returns: the zero-based Integer index of the first match, or nil if none

function replace(s, pattern, replacement) ¶

Returns a copy of s with every (non-overlapping) occurrence of pattern replaced by replacement.

String.replace("a-b-c", "-", "_")   # == "a_b_c"
s
the string to rewrite
pattern
the substring to replace
replacement
the string to substitute for each pattern

Returns: a new String with every pattern replaced by replacement

function split(s, sep) ¶

Splits s at each occurrence of sep, returning a list of parts. Empty sep splits into one-character strings. To rejoin, use List.join.

String.split("a,b,c", ",")   # == ["a", "b", "c"]
s
the string to split
sep
the separator to split on ("" splits into characters)

Returns: a List of the String parts

function upcase(s) ¶

Returns s with each ASCII letter uppercased.

String.upcase("hello")   # == "HELLO"
s
the string to uppercase

Returns: a new String with each ASCII letter uppercased

function downcase(s) ¶

Returns s with each ASCII letter lowercased.

String.downcase("HELLO")   # == "hello"
s
the string to lowercase

Returns: a new String with each ASCII letter lowercased

function trim(s) ¶

Returns s with leading and trailing whitespace removed.

String.trim("  hi  ")   # == "hi"
s
the string to trim

Returns: a new String without leading or trailing whitespace

function trim_left(s) ¶

Returns s with leading whitespace removed.

String.trim_left("  hi  ")   # == "hi  "
s
the string to trim

Returns: a new String without leading whitespace

function trim_right(s) ¶

Returns s with trailing whitespace removed.

String.trim_right("  hi  ")   # == "  hi"
s
the string to trim

Returns: a new String without trailing whitespace

function reverse(s) ¶

Returns s with its characters in reverse order.

String.reverse("hello")   # == "olleh"
s
the string to reverse

Returns: a new String with the code points of s in reverse order

function repeat(s, n) ¶

Returns s concatenated with itself n times. n <= 0 yields "".

String.repeat("ab", 3)   # == "ababab"
s
the string to repeat
n
how many times to repeat s

Returns: a new String of s repeated n times ("" when n <= 0)

function to_list(s) ¶

Splits s into a list of single-character strings, one per Unicode code point. The inverse of from_list.

String.to_list("abc")   # == ["a", "b", "c"]
s
the string to explode

Returns: a List of single-character Strings, one per code point

function pad_left(s, width, pad_char) ¶

Returns s left-padded with pad_char until it reaches at least width characters. Already-long-enough s comes back unchanged. pad_char is a single character; a longer one may overshoot width.

String.pad_left("7", 3, "0")     # == "007"
String.pad_left("hello", 3, "0") # == "hello"
s

width
the minimum length of the result
pad_char
the single-character string to pad with

Returns: s, left-padded to at least width characters

function pad_right(s, width, pad_char) ¶

Returns s right-padded with pad_char until it reaches at least width characters. Already-long-enough s comes back unchanged. pad_char is a single character; a longer one may overshoot width.

String.pad_right("7", 3, "0")     # == "700"
String.pad_right("hello", 3, "0") # == "hello"
s
the string to pad
width
the minimum length of the result
pad_char
the single-character string to pad with

Returns: s, right-padded to at least width characters

function capitalize(s) ¶

Returns s with its first character uppercased and the rest lowercased. "" comes back unchanged.

String.capitalize("hello WORLD")   # == "Hello world"
String.capitalize("")              # == ""
s

Returns: a new String, first character up, rest down

function from_list(chars) ¶

Concatenates a list of single-character strings into one string. The inverse of to_list.

String.from_list(["a", "b", "c"])   # == "abc"
