(private) n rendered as decimal digits, left-padded with zeros to at least width characters. Backs offset_text.

DateTime.title: DateTime — Ramos
DateTime.heading: DateTime
DateTime.body:
Summary

DateTime — a NaiveDateTime plus a fixed offset from UTC, so it names a precise instant rather than just a wall-clock reading.

Module documentation

DateTime — a NaiveDateTime plus a fixed offset from UTC, so it names a precise instant rather than just a wall-clock reading.

There is no time zone database here (no dependency ships one) — an offset_minutes is a plain number, like -300 for UTC-5 or 330 for UTC+5:30, not a zone name that shifts with daylight saving. The fields (year..millisecond) are the local reading at that offset:

utc = DateTime.now()
ny = DateTime.now_at(-300)
utc.offset_minutes   # == 0
ny.offset_minutes    # == -300

Two DateTimes at different offsets can still name the same instant — compare and diff_millis account for the offset, so they agree with what a clock actually measures, not just the printed fields:

a = DateTime.new(2024, 1, 1, 12, 0, 0, 0)     # noon UTC
b = DateTime.new(2024, 1, 1, 7, 0, 0, -300)   # 07:00 at UTC-5 — the same instant
DateTime.compare(a, b)   # == 0

== does not know this — it compares fields structurally like any other struct, so a == b above is false even though they name one instant. Convert with with_offset (or to_utc) before comparing fields directly.

now_in and in_time_zone take a TimeZone (a name plus a fixed offset) rather than a bare number, when a name is worth carrying:

ist = TimeZone.fixed("IST", 330)
DateTime.now_in(ist).offset_minutes   # == 330

Conventions:

  • compare orders by instant (the UTC equivalent), not by the printed local fields.
  • to_iso renders the offset as Z for UTC or ±HH:MM otherwise (via TimeZone.offset_text), and parse reads the same shape back.
  • see NaiveDateTime for the zone-free version of this shape, Date for the calendar day alone, and TimeZone for the named-offset type.

Functions

function new(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, offset_minutes) Builds a DateTime from local fields at offset_minutes from UTC, with millisecond: 0. Every field past year normalizes when it overflows or underflows its natural range, the same way Date.new's day does.
function now() The current instant, as UTC (offset_minutes: 0).
function now_at(offset_minutes) The current instant, as local fields at offset_minutes from UTC.
function now_in(time_zone) The current instant, as local fields in time_zone.
function from_epoch_millis(utc_ms, offset_minutes) The DateTime for the instant utc_ms milliseconds after the epoch, with its fields expressed at offset_minutes from UTC.
helper from_epoch_millis_raw(utc_ms, offset_minutes) (private) from_epoch_millis's own body, so shift can reach it without calling the public function.
function from_naive(naive, offset_minutes) Tags a NaiveDateTime's fields as the local time at offset_minutes — a relabeling, not a conversion: the fields are copied as they are.
function parse(text) Parses "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS±HH:MM" (or a trailing "Z" for UTC) — either a T or a plain space between the date and the time, as to_iso renders or as the U"..." sigil is written. The seconds' fractional part is optional and any number of digits (padded or truncated to milliseconds), the same as NaiveDateTime.parse.
function date(self) The Date half of self's local reading, dropping the time of day and the offset.
function to_naive(self) self's local fields as a NaiveDateTime, dropping the offset.
function to_utc_epoch_millis(self) The instant self names, as milliseconds since the epoch (UTC) — the bridge to arithmetic and comparison, and what makes two DateTimes at different offsets comparable.
function to_utc(self) The same instant as self, with its fields expressed at UTC (offset_minutes: 0).
function with_offset(self, offset_minutes) The same instant as self, with its fields re-expressed at offset_minutes — the way to convert between offsets.
function in_time_zone(self, time_zone) The same instant as self, with its fields re-expressed at time_zone's offset — with_offset, taking a TimeZone instead of a bare number.
function time_zone(self) self's offset as a TimeZone, named after the offset itself ("UTC" at 0, otherwise ±HH:MM) — self only ever keeps the number, never the name a zone arrived with.
function to_iso(self) self rendered as "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmm" followed by Z (when offset_minutes is 0) or a signed ±HH:MM offset.
function add_days(self, n) self shifted by n days, keeping the offset.
function add_weeks(self, n) self shifted by n weeks (n * 7 days), keeping the offset.
function add_months(self, n) self shifted by n months, keeping the time of day and the offset — Date.add_months applied to the local date half, with the day-overflow normalization that implies.
function add_hours(self, n) self shifted by n hours, keeping the offset.
function add_minutes(self, n) self shifted by n minutes, keeping the offset.
function add_seconds(self, n) self shifted by n seconds, keeping the offset.
function compare(self, other) Orders two date-times by the instant they name (their UTC equivalent), as -1, 0 or 1 — not by their printed local fields, so two DateTimes at different offsets compare correctly.

helper pad(n, width) (private) n rendered as decimal digits, left-padded with zeros to at least width characters. Backs to_iso.

Builds a DateTime from local fields at offset_minutes from UTC, with millisecond: 0. Every field past year normalizes when it overflows or underflows its natural range, the same way Date.new's day does.

DateTime.new(2024, 2, 9, 13, 45, 30, 0)

function from_naive(naive, offset_minutes) ¶

Tags a NaiveDateTime's fields as the local time at offset_minutes — a relabeling, not a conversion: the fields are copied as they are.

Returns: a NaiveDateTime with the same local fields

function to_utc_epoch_millis(self) ¶

The instant self names, as milliseconds since the epoch (UTC) — the bridge to arithmetic and comparison, and what makes two DateTimes at different offsets comparable.

DateTime.to_utc_epoch_millis(DateTime{year: 1970, month: 1, day: 1, hour: 1, offset_minutes: 60})   # == 0
self
the date-time to convert

Returns: an Integer millisecond count, negative before the epoch

function to_utc(self) ¶

The same instant as self, with its fields expressed at UTC (offset_minutes: 0).

DateTime.to_utc(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 8, offset_minutes: -300})
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 13, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the date-time to convert

Returns: an equivalent DateTime at offset_minutes: 0

function with_offset(self, offset_minutes) ¶

The same instant as self, with its fields re-expressed at offset_minutes — the way to convert between offsets.

DateTime.with_offset(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 13, offset_minutes: 0}, -300)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 8, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: -300}
self
the date-time to convert
offset_minutes
the offset from UTC to render the fields at

Returns: an equivalent DateTime at the new offset

function in_time_zone(self, time_zone) ¶

The same instant as self, with its fields re-expressed at time_zone's offset — with_offset, taking a TimeZone instead of a bare number.

DateTime.in_time_zone(DateTime{offset_minutes: 0}, TimeZone.fixed("IST", 330)).offset_minutes   # == 330
self
the date-time to convert
time_zone
the TimeZone to render the fields in

Returns: an equivalent DateTime at that zone's offset

function time_zone(self) ¶

self's offset as a TimeZone, named after the offset itself ("UTC" at 0, otherwise ±HH:MM) — self only ever keeps the number, never the name a zone arrived with.

DateTime.time_zone(DateTime{offset_minutes: -300}).name   # == "-05:00"
self
the date-time to read

Returns: a TimeZone matching self's offset

function to_iso(self) ¶

self rendered as "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmm" followed by Z (when offset_minutes is 0) or a signed ±HH:MM offset.

DateTime.to_iso(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 3, minute: 5, second: 9, millisecond: 7, offset_minutes: 0})
# == "2024-02-09T03:05:09.007Z"
DateTime.to_iso(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 3, minute: 5, second: 9, millisecond: 7, offset_minutes: -300})
# == "2024-02-09T03:05:09.007-05:00"
self
the date-time to render

Returns: the ISO-8601 string

function add_days(self, n) ¶

self shifted by n days, keeping the offset.

DateTime.add_days(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 28, hour: 12}, 1)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 29, hour: 12, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the starting date-time
n
how many days to add (negative subtracts)

Returns: a new DateTime

function add_weeks(self, n) ¶

self shifted by n weeks (n * 7 days), keeping the offset.

DateTime.add_weeks(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 1, day: 1, hour: 12}, 1)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 1, day: 8, hour: 12, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the starting date-time
n
how many weeks to add (negative subtracts)

Returns: a new DateTime

function add_months(self, n) ¶

self shifted by n months, keeping the time of day and the offset — Date.add_months applied to the local date half, with the day-overflow normalization that implies.

DateTime.add_months(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 1, day: 15, hour: 12}, 1)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 15, hour: 12, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the starting date-time
n
how many months to add (negative subtracts)

Returns: a new DateTime

function add_hours(self, n) ¶

self shifted by n hours, keeping the offset.

DateTime.add_hours(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 23}, 2)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 10, hour: 1, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the starting date-time
n
how many hours to add (negative subtracts)

Returns: a new DateTime

function add_minutes(self, n) ¶

self shifted by n minutes, keeping the offset.

DateTime.add_minutes(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 0, minute: 30}, 45)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, hour: 1, minute: 15, second: 0, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the starting date-time
n
how many minutes to add (negative subtracts)

Returns: a new DateTime

function add_seconds(self, n) ¶

self shifted by n seconds, keeping the offset.

DateTime.add_seconds(DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, second: 45}, 30)
# == DateTime{year: 2024, month: 2, day: 9, minute: 1, second: 15, millisecond: 0, offset_minutes: 0}
self
the starting date-time
n
how many seconds to add (negative subtracts)

Returns: a new DateTime

function compare(self, other) ¶

Orders two date-times by the instant they name (their UTC equivalent), as -1, 0 or 1 — not by their printed local fields, so two DateTimes at different offsets compare correctly.

DateTime.compare(DateTime{hour: 1}, DateTime{hour: 2})                        # == -1
DateTime.compare(DateTime{hour: 12}, DateTime{hour: 7, offset_minutes: -300})  # == 0
self
the first date-time
other
the second date-time

Returns: -1 when self is earlier, 1 when later, 0 when equal

function diff_millis(self, other) ¶

The number of milliseconds from the instant other names to the one self names — positive when self is later, negative when earlier.

DateTime.diff_millis(DateTime{second: 10}, DateTime{second: 1})   # == 9000
self
the later (or earlier) date-time
other
the date-time to measure from

Returns: an Integer millisecond count

function day_of_week(self) ¶

The day of the week self's local date falls on. Delegates to Date.day_of_week.

`:thursday`, `:friday`, `:saturday`
DateTime.day_of_week(DateTime{year: 1970, month: 1, day: 1})   # == :thursday
self
the date-time to inspect

Returns: one of :sunday, :monday, :tuesday, :wednesday,

helper raw_millis(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, millisecond) private ¶

(private) Milliseconds since the epoch for the given fields, as if they were UTC — before the offset is applied. Shared arithmetic behind new, parse and to_utc_epoch_millis.

helper shift(self, millis) private ¶

(private) self moved by millis milliseconds of real time, keeping its offset. Backs the add_* family.

helper floor_div(a, b) private ¶

(private) a divided by b, rounding toward negative infinity — unlike /, which truncates toward zero. b is assumed positive.

helper offset_start(rest) private ¶

(private) The index in rest (the text after the date) where its offset begins — the trailing "Z", or the +/- of a ±HH:MM. The clock text before it never contains any of those three characters, so whichever appears first is unambiguous. Backs parse.

helper millis_from_fraction(digits) private ¶

(private) A fractional-second string of any length as milliseconds: "5" is 500, "123456" truncates to 123. Backs parse.

helper pad(n, width) private ¶

(private) n rendered as decimal digits, left-padded with zeros to at least width characters. Backs to_iso.

File.title: File — Ramos
File.heading: File
File.body:
Summary

File — reading, writing, and managing files on the host filesystem.

Module documentation

File — reading, writing, and managing files on the host filesystem.

This is Ramos's window onto mutable state: files change over time. Every function here is therefore effectful and reports success or failure as a value you pattern match, never by raising:

  • fallible operations return (:ok, value), or an error built by error
  • operations with nothing to hand back return the bare :ok
  • exists and is_file return a plain true/false

A failure is (:error, (reason, message, stacktrace)). reason is a lowercase symbol straight from the OS — :enoent (no such file), :eacces (permission denied), :eexist, :io_error, or :unsupported — the same vocabulary a bare reason would use, but a symbol alone does not say which path failed, so message names both: "reading file \config.txt\ failed with :enoent". Branches read cleanly:

case File.read("config.txt")
  (:ok, text) -> parse(text)
  (:error, (:enoent, _, _)) -> :use_defaults
  (:error, (reason, message, _)) -> (:error, (:config_unreadable, message))

Every function takes a path; there are no open file handles. read and write move the whole file at once, which keeps the model simple and the values immutable.

Conventions:

  • paths are host-native strings; relative paths resolve against the cwd.
  • write truncates; append adds to the end; both create the file if it is missing.
  • mv is the one way to move a file: it tries a rename first and falls back to copy + delete, so it works across filesystems.

Functions

function read(path) Reads the entire file at path into a string.
function write(path, contents) Writes contents to path, replacing any existing content and creating the file if it does not exist.
function append(path, contents) Appends contents to the end of path, creating the file if it does not exist. Unlike write, existing content is preserved.
function size(path) Returns the size of path in bytes.
function rm(path) Deletes the file at path.
function cp(source, dest) Copies the file at source to dest, overwriting dest if it exists.
function mv(source, dest) Moves the file at source to dest. Works across filesystems: it tries a rename first, then falls back to a copy followed by deleting source.
function exists(path) Returns true if something exists at path (a file or a directory), else false. Use is_file to require that it is a regular file.
function is_file(path) Returns true if path exists and is a regular file, else false (including when path is a directory or does not exist).
function touch(path) Creates path if it does not exist, and updates its modified time to now. Existing content is preserved — the file-manager equivalent of touch(1).
function chmod(path, mode) Sets the permission bits of path. mode is the numeric permission — for example 493 is rwxr-xr-x and 420 is rw-r--r--.
helper wrap(result, action) (private) Turns a native (:error, reason) into an error built by error: the reason stays the same symbol, but the message names the path action describes together with it, since a bare :enoent alone does not say which file failed. Anything else — :ok, or (:ok, value) — passes through unchanged.

function read(path) ¶

Reads the entire file at path into a string.

read
File.write("greeting.txt", "hello\n")
File.read("greeting.txt")   # == (:ok, "hello\n")
(:error, (type, message, _)) = File.read("missing.txt")
(type, message)   # == (:enoent, "reading file `missing.txt` failed with :enoent")
path
the path to read

Returns: (:ok, contents), or an error built by error if it cannot be

function write(path, contents) ¶

Writes contents to path, replacing any existing content and creating the file if it does not exist.

File.write("out.txt", "hello\n")   # == :ok
path
the path to write
contents
the string to write

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error on failure

function append(path, contents) ¶

Appends contents to the end of path, creating the file if it does not exist. Unlike write, existing content is preserved.

File.append("log.txt", "another line\n")   # == :ok
path
the path to append to
contents
the string to append

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error on failure

function size(path) ¶

Returns the size of path in bytes.

File.write("greeting.txt", "hello\n")
File.size("greeting.txt")   # == (:ok, 6)
path
the path to measure

Returns: (:ok, bytes), or an error built by error if it cannot be read

function rm(path) ¶

Deletes the file at path.

there)
File.write("out.txt", "bye\n")
File.rm("out.txt")   # == :ok
path
the path to delete

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error (e.g. :enoent if it is not

function cp(source, dest) ¶

Copies the file at source to dest, overwriting dest if it exists.

File.write("a.txt", "hello\n")
File.cp("a.txt", "b.txt")   # == :ok
source
the file to copy from
dest
the path to copy to

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error on failure

function mv(source, dest) ¶

Moves the file at source to dest. Works across filesystems: it tries a rename first, then falls back to a copy followed by deleting source.

File.write("draft.txt", "hello\n")
File.mv("draft.txt", "final.txt")   # == :ok
source
the file to move from
dest
the path to move to

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error on failure

function exists(path) ¶

Returns true if something exists at path (a file or a directory), else false. Use is_file to require that it is a regular file.

File.write("out.txt", "hello\n")
File.exists("out.txt")   # == true
File.exists("missing")   # == false
path
the path to test

Returns: true if path exists, else false

function is_file(path) ¶

Returns true if path exists and is a regular file, else false (including when path is a directory or does not exist).

File.write("out.txt", "hello\n")
Dir.mkdir("src")
File.is_file("out.txt")   # == true
File.is_file("src")       # == false
path
the path to test

Returns: true if path is a regular file, else false

function touch(path) ¶

Creates path if it does not exist, and updates its modified time to now. Existing content is preserved — the file-manager equivalent of touch(1).

File.touch("build.stamp")   # == :ok
path
the path to touch

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error on failure

function chmod(path, mode) ¶

Sets the permission bits of path. mode is the numeric permission — for example 493 is rwxr-xr-x and 420 is rw-r--r--.

Unix
File.write("run.sh", "echo hi\n")
File.chmod("run.sh", 493)   # == :ok
path
the path to change
mode
the numeric permission bits

Returns: :ok, an error built by error, or an :unsupported error off

helper wrap(result, action) private ¶

(private) Turns a native (:error, reason) into an error built by error: the reason stays the same symbol, but the message names the path action describes together with it, since a bare :enoent alone does not say which file failed. Anything else — :ok, or (:ok, value) — passes through unchanged.

Dir.title: Dir — Ramos
Dir.heading: Dir
Dir.body:
Summary

Dir — inspecting and manipulating directories on the host filesystem.

Module documentation

Dir — inspecting and manipulating directories on the host filesystem.

Like File, every function here is effectful and reports outcome as a value you pattern match rather than by raising:

  • fallible operations return (:ok, value) or (:error, reason)
  • operations with nothing to hand back return the bare :ok
  • exists and is_dir return a plain true/false

reason is a lowercase symbol — :enoent (no such directory), :eacces (permission denied), :eexist, or :io_error:

case Dir.ls("src")
  (:ok, entries) -> List.each(entries, do e -> print(e))
  (:error, :enoent) -> print("no such directory")
  (:error, reason) -> (:error, (:dir_failed, reason))

The current working directory is process-wide state: cd changes it for every later relative path (in Dir and File alike), and cwd reads it.

Conventions:

  • paths are host-native strings; relative paths resolve against the cwd.
  • ls returns bare entry names (not full paths), sorted.
  • mkdir creates parent directories as needed and is happy if the directory already exists.

Functions

function cwd() Returns the process's current working directory.
function cd(path) Changes the process's current working directory to path. Affects every relative path used afterwards, in both Dir and File.
function mkdir(path) Creates the directory at path, including any missing parent directories (like mkdir -p). Succeeds if the directory already exists.
function ls(path) Lists the entries of the directory at path — the bare names of the files and subdirectories it contains (not full paths), sorted.
function exists(path) Returns true if something exists at path (a file or a directory), else false. Use is_dir to require that it is a directory.
function is_dir(path) Returns true if path exists and is a directory, else false (including when path is a regular file or does not exist).

function cwd() ¶

Returns the process's current working directory.

Dir.cwd()   # (:ok, "/home/andrew/dev/ramos") — whatever it happens to be

Returns: (:ok, path), or (:error, reason) if it cannot be determined

function cd(path) ¶

Changes the process's current working directory to path. Affects every relative path used afterwards, in both Dir and File.

Dir.mkdir("src")
Dir.cd("src")   # == :ok
path
the directory to change into

Returns: :ok, or (:error, reason) (e.g. :enoent) on failure

function mkdir(path) ¶

Creates the directory at path, including any missing parent directories (like mkdir -p). Succeeds if the directory already exists.

Dir.mkdir("build/cache")   # == :ok
path
the directory to create

Returns: :ok, or (:error, reason) on failure

function ls(path) ¶

Lists the entries of the directory at path — the bare names of the files and subdirectories it contains (not full paths), sorted.

Dir.mkdir("stdlib")
File.write("stdlib/dir.rmo", "")
File.write("stdlib/file.rmo", "")
Dir.ls("stdlib")   # == (:ok, ["dir.rmo", "file.rmo"])
path
the directory to list

Returns: (:ok, names) (a sorted list of strings), or (:error, reason)

function exists(path) ¶

Returns true if something exists at path (a file or a directory), else false. Use is_dir to require that it is a directory.

Dir.mkdir("stdlib")
Dir.exists("stdlib")   # == true
Dir.exists("missing")  # == false
path
the path to test

Returns: true if path exists, else false

function is_dir(path) ¶

Returns true if path exists and is a directory, else false (including when path is a regular file or does not exist).

Dir.mkdir("stdlib")
File.write("stdlib/dir.rmo", "")
Dir.is_dir("stdlib")           # == true
Dir.is_dir("stdlib/dir.rmo")  # == false
path
the path to test

Returns: true if path is a directory, else false

Socket.title: Socket — Ramos
Socket.heading: Socket
Socket.body:
Summary

Socket — one open TCP connection: the reading and writing half of a connection, whichever side opened it.

Module documentation

Socket — one open TCP connection: the reading and writing half of a connection, whichever side opened it.

A Socket comes from one of two places: connect, dialing out to a listening peer, or ServerSocket.accept, handed one by a peer that dialed in. From there the two are identical — the same send, recv, and close work on either:

(:ok, socket) = Socket.connect("example.com", 9000)
Socket.send(socket, "GET /\n")
Socket.recv(socket, 1024)
Socket.close(socket)

Every operation blocks: connect waits for the handshake, send waits for the write to complete, recv waits until at least one byte has arrived. There is no timeout and no non-blocking mode — pair a blocking call with Thread (see [Threads](#threads) in the guide) when it needs to run alongside other work, the same way the examples on this page pair connect with a listening ServerSocket.accept.

recv reads bytes, not lines or messages. TCP has no framing of its own — one send may arrive as several recvs, or several sends as one — so a protocol that needs message boundaries (a length prefix, a delimiter, a fixed size) has to add them itself. recv(socket, n) reads up to n bytes, however many are available already; call it again for more. It returns (:ok, "") exactly when the peer has closed its side — a blocking read otherwise never comes back with zero bytes.

Every fallible operation here follows File's convention: (:ok, value) or a bare :ok on success, an error built by error on failure, its type a lowercase symbol from the OS (:econnrefused, :etimedout, …). close is idempotent and safe to call from whichever side gives up first — the other side's next send or recv then fails with :econnreset or (:ok, "") rather than hanging.

Functions

function connect(host, port) Opens a TCP connection to host:port, blocking until the handshake completes.
function send(socket, data) Writes data to the connection, blocking until every byte has been handed to the OS.
function recv(socket, size) Reads up to size bytes from the connection, blocking until at least one has arrived. May return fewer than size bytes — it never waits for more once some have shown up.
function peer_address(socket) The address of the peer this socket is connected to.
function close(socket) Closes the connection. The peer's next recv sees end of stream; its next send fails. Closing twice is not an error.
helper wrap(result, action) (private) Same convention as File's wrap: turns a native (:error, reason) into an error built by error, whose message names action alongside the reason. Anything else — :ok, or (:ok, value) — passes through unchanged.

function connect(host, port) ¶

Opens a TCP connection to host:port, blocking until the handshake completes.

`:econnrefused` when nothing is listening
(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
(:ok, socket) = Socket.connect("127.0.0.1", port)
Socket.close(socket)   # == :ok
host
the address to connect to — a hostname or an IP
port
the port to connect to

Returns: (:ok, socket), or an error built by error on failure — e.g.

function send(socket, data) ¶

Writes data to the connection, blocking until every byte has been handed to the OS.

(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
t = Thread.start(do -> Socket.connect("127.0.0.1", port))
(:ok, conn) = ServerSocket.accept(server)
(:ok, client) = Thread.await(t)
Socket.send(client, "hello")   # == :ok
Socket.recv(conn, 5)           # == (:ok, "hello")
socket
a Socket from connect or ServerSocket.accept
data
the String to write

Returns: :ok, or an error built by error on failure

function recv(socket, size) ¶

Reads up to size bytes from the connection, blocking until at least one has arrived. May return fewer than size bytes — it never waits for more once some have shown up.

the connection — or an error built by `error` on failure
(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
t = Thread.start(do -> Socket.connect("127.0.0.1", port))
(:ok, conn) = ServerSocket.accept(server)
(:ok, client) = Thread.await(t)
Socket.send(conn, "hi")
Socket.recv(client, 1024)   # == (:ok, "hi")
socket
a Socket from connect or ServerSocket.accept
size
the most bytes to read

Returns: (:ok, data) — data is "" exactly when the peer has closed

function peer_address(socket) ¶

The address of the peer this socket is connected to.

(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
(:ok, socket) = Socket.connect("127.0.0.1", port)
(:ok, addr) = Socket.peer_address(socket)
addr   # == "127.0.0.1:#{port}"
socket
a Socket from connect or ServerSocket.accept

Returns: (:ok, "ip:port"), or an error built by error on failure

function close(socket) ¶

Closes the connection. The peer's next recv sees end of stream; its next send fails. Closing twice is not an error.

(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
(:ok, socket) = Socket.connect("127.0.0.1", port)
Socket.close(socket)   # == :ok
Socket.close(socket)   # == :ok
socket
a Socket from connect or ServerSocket.accept

Returns: :ok

helper wrap(result, action) private ¶

(private) Same convention as File's wrap: turns a native (:error, reason) into an error built by error, whose message names action alongside the reason. Anything else — :ok, or (:ok, value) — passes through unchanged.

ServerSocket.title: ServerSocket — Ramos
ServerSocket.heading: ServerSocket
ServerSocket.body:
Summary

ServerSocket — a bound, listening TCP socket: the acceptor half of a connection.

Module documentation

ServerSocket — a bound, listening TCP socket: the acceptor half of a connection.

bind claims a host and port and starts listening; accept blocks until a client connects and hands back the Socket for that one connection. Reading and writing never happen on the listener itself — only on the Sockets it produces:

(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 9000)
(:ok, conn) = ServerSocket.accept(server)   # blocks for a client
Socket.recv(conn, 1024)

Binding port 0 asks the OS to pick a free port instead of naming one — local_port reports what it chose. That is how this module's own examples avoid clashing with whatever else is listening on the machine running them.

accept is blocking and one connection at a time; there is no select and no non-blocking mode. To serve more than one client at once, hand each accepted Socket off to its own Thread.start and loop back to accept for the next:

handle = do socket ->
  Socket.send(socket, Socket.recv(socket, 1024))
  Socket.close(socket)
loop = do server ->
  (:ok, socket) = ServerSocket.accept(server)
  Thread.start(do -> handle(socket))
  loop(server)

Every fallible operation here follows File's convention: (:ok, value) or a bare :ok on success, an error built by error on failure, its type a lowercase symbol from the OS (:eaddrinuse, :eacces, …).

Functions

function bind(host, port) Binds to host:port and starts listening for connections.
function accept(server) Blocks until a client connects, then returns the Socket for that one connection. Call it again to accept the next.
function local_port(server) The port bind ended up listening on: the number passed in, unless it was 0, in which case this is what the OS chose.
function close(server) Stops listening and releases the port. Sockets already handed out by accept are unaffected. Closing twice is not an error.
helper wrap(result, action) (private) Same convention as File's wrap: turns a native (:error, reason) into an error built by error, whose message names action alongside the reason — a bare :eaddrinuse does not say which bind failed. Anything else — :ok, or (:ok, value) — passes through unchanged.

function bind(host, port) ¶

Binds to host:port and starts listening for connections.

read its choice back with `local_port`
`:eaddrinuse` when the port is already taken
(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
ServerSocket.close(server)   # == :ok
host
the address to bind, e.g. "127.0.0.1" or "0.0.0.0"
port
the port to bind, or 0 to let the OS choose a free one —

Returns: (:ok, server), or an error built by error on failure — e.g.

function accept(server) ¶

Blocks until a client connects, then returns the Socket for that one connection. Call it again to accept the next.

(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
t = Thread.start(do -> Socket.connect("127.0.0.1", port))
(:ok, conn) = ServerSocket.accept(server)
(:ok, client) = Thread.await(t)
Socket.close(conn)
Socket.close(client)   # == :ok
server
a ServerSocket from bind

Returns: (:ok, socket), or an error built by error on failure

function local_port(server) ¶

The port bind ended up listening on: the number passed in, unless it was 0, in which case this is what the OS chose.

(:ok, server) = ServerSocket.bind("127.0.0.1", 0)
(:ok, port) = ServerSocket.local_port(server)
port > 0   # == true
server

HttpServer.title: HttpServer — Ramos
HttpServer.heading: HttpServer
HttpServer.body:
Summary

HttpServer — a minimal, bounded-concurrency HTTP server built on Socket/ServerSocket, with a Pool capping how many connections it ever handles at once.

Module documentation

HttpServer — a minimal, bounded-concurrency HTTP server built on Socket/ServerSocket, with a Pool capping how many connections it ever handles at once.

handler =
  do request, socket
    body = "hi"
    HttpResponse.new(socket)
    | HttpResponse.put_header("Content-Length", "#{String.length(body)}")
    | HttpResponse.send_chunk(body)
HttpServer{port: 8080}.start(handler)

start binds the port, then loops forever: accept a connection, hand it off to its own Thread to be read, run through the lambda it was given, and closed — and immediately accept the next, up to max_connections at a time. There is no framework here — no routing, no parsing of the request line or headers, no status-line helpers. The lambda gets raw request text and the raw Socket in, and writes the response straight to that socket itself, typically through HttpResponse (see its own doc):

handler =
  do request, socket
    response =
      case String.starts_with(request, "GET / ")
        true -> HttpResponse.new(socket)
        false -> HttpResponse.new(socket).set_status(404)
    response
    | HttpResponse.put_header("Content-Length", "2")
    | HttpResponse.send_chunk("hi")
HttpServer{port: 8080}.start(handler)

The lambda's return value is ignored. Whatever reaches the client is exactly what the lambda wrote to socket itself, nothing more — unlike the old contract where a returned string was the response, writing (or not) is now entirely the lambda's own doing. A handler that writes nothing sends nothing back; the connection still closes once the lambda returns (see below), same as any other request.

What "the request text" is. Socket.recv reads bytes, not messages — see its own doc — so this reads chunks until the blank line that ends the headers ("\r\n\r\n") shows up, and hands back everything read up to and including it. That is the whole request for a bodyless GET/HEAD/ DELETE; a request with a body (a POST, typically) arrives with its body cut off at the blank line, since nothing here reads Content-Length bytes of body on top of the headers. Reading a body, if the handler needs one, is on the lambda — parse Content-Length out of what it was given and Socket.recv the rest off the connection itself (see the doc on start for how to reach it).

One request per connection. There is no keep-alive: the connection closes right after the response is written, whether or not the request asked to keep it open.

Each connection runs on its own Thread, up to max_connections at once. accept hands a connection to a freshly started thread — the reading and the call to the lambda, which writes its own response to the socket it was handed, all happen there — and goes straight back to waiting for the next client, so a slow lambda or a client that trickles its request in slowly only holds up that one connection, not the others behind it. A Pool (see its own module doc) tracks how many are in flight: max_connections plain integer "slots", checkin before a connection is even accepted, checkout once its thread finishes. Once every slot is taken, accept itself blocks — no new connection is accepted, and no new thread starts — until one frees up. That is the whole difference from the naive version of this: without a cap, a burst of connections is a burst of threads with nothing to stop it; with one, the thread count has a hard ceiling and the excess queues in the OS's own backlog instead of becoming live threads.

That is not free either, and is worth knowing before it surprises you:

  • Slots are freed oldest-first, not first-to-finish. There is no "whichever thread finishes first" primitive to build the fairer version out of, so freeing a slot waits on the oldest still-open connection specifically, however many newer ones already finished. Ordinarily that is invisible — connections finish in roughly the order they started. But a single connection that never finishes (see "no read timeout" below) is a problem the moment every slot fills up: accept needs the oldest one to free a slot, the oldest one is the stuck one, and now nothing is ever accepted again, no matter how fast every other connection finishes. One stuck client is enough to stall the entire server once the pool behind it is full.
  • A connection's thread is never awaited by whatever serves it — only by the accept loop reclaiming its slot, later, possibly long after the thread itself finished. An uncaught error inside the lambda still only ends that one thread, not the whole server (see Thread's own doc for why), but it is still not reported anywhere; a lambda that wants its failures seen has to report them itself.
  • Still no read timeout. A connection that never finishes sending its headers ties up its own thread and its own pool slot — bounded now, rather than unbounded, but see the head-of-line point above for what one such connection can still do once the pool is full.

None of this makes HttpServer hardened for hostile traffic — there is still no timeout — but the thread count now has a hard ceiling, which was the sharper problem.

A request is capped at 64 KB of headers. Past that, whatever was read so far is handed to the lambda as-is (almost certainly not ending in "\r\n\r\n") rather than growing without bound — a defense against a client that never sends the blank line, not a real HTTP limit.

Functions

function new(port, max_connections) Builds an HttpServer, validating both fields up front — the same role Date.new plays over a bare Date{...} literal. The plain HttpServer{port: 8080} literal still works and still defaults max_connections to 100; new is for when you want both checked (and both named) at construction time rather than failing later, inside start.
function start(self, f) Binds self.port and serves connections forever: accept, hand the connection to its own Thread — which reads the request, calls f(request, socket) (the lambda writes its own response to socket, typically through HttpResponse), and closes — and immediately accept the next, up to self.max_connections at a time; past that, accept itself waits for one to free up rather than starting another thread. The accept loop runs on the calling thread and does not return under normal operation; each connection's handling happens elsewhere and in parallel — see the module doc for what "the request" contains, how the cap works, and what is and is not handled for you.

HttpRequest.title: HttpRequest — Ramos
HttpRequest.heading: HttpRequest
HttpRequest.body:
Summary

HttpRequest — parses raw HTTP request text into its request line, headers, and body. The natural companion to HttpServer, whose handler lambda receives exactly this text (see that module's doc for what "the request text" contains and does not contain):

Module documentation

HttpRequest — parses raw HTTP request text into its request line, headers, and body. The natural companion to HttpServer, whose handler lambda receives exactly this text (see that module's doc for what "the request text" contains and does not contain):

HttpServer{port: 8080}.start(do text -> handle(HttpRequest.new(text)))

new is the only way in:

request = HttpRequest.new("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
request.method    # == "GET"
request.path      # == "/hello"
request.version   # == "HTTP/1.1"
request.headers   # == [("host", "localhost")]

headers is a List of (name, value) string tuples, not a Map. HTTP allows the same header name more than once — Set-Cookie in a response, Cookie or X-Forwarded-For in a request — with every occurrence significant, so a Map would silently drop all but one. Find one by name with List.find:

headers = [("host", "localhost"), ("x-test", "a")]
match_host =
  do header
    (name, _) = header
    name == "host"
List.find(headers, match_host)
# == ("host", "localhost")

Every name in headers is downcased — "Host" and "HOST" on the wire both come back "host" — since HTTP header names are case-insensitive by spec and one written form beats guessing which of several a caller might match against. Only the name changes; a value is kept exactly as sent.

The request line splits on single spaces, exactly three tokens. That is what every conforming client sends — the request-target is percent-encoded specifically so it never contains a literal space — so a request line shaped any other way fails loudly, an assert, rather than silently producing a half-parsed HttpRequest.

request_body is whatever text follows the blank line ("\r\n\r\n") that ends the headers — "" if text has no such blank line (an incomplete read) or nothing after it. HttpServer itself only reads up through that blank line, not a Content-Length body on top of it (see its own doc) — a handler that needs the body reads it off the connection itself and hands HttpRequest.new the two concatenated.

Query-string parameters are parsed lazily, from path, not eagerly in new. get_query_params/get_query_param parse path's "?" suffix on every call rather than something new computes up front — there is nowhere on an immutable struct to cache the result, so a request whose handler never reads a query parameter never pays to parse one. Unlike headers, a repeated query key has no protocol meaning to preserve, so this one comes back as a Map — last occurrence wins — decoded the way application/x-www-form-urlencoded decodes it (+ to space, %XX to the byte it names).

A JSON body is get_json_params, not get_query_params. It checks Content-Type for a .../json media type before parsing request_body with Json — a missing or non-JSON Content-Type, or a body Json cannot parse, all come back nil rather than raising.

A form body is get_form_params. Plain <form> posts (no file input) send application/x-www-form-urlencoded, the same encoding as a query string, just in request_body instead of path; get_form_params checks Content-Type for it and decodes the body exactly as get_query_params decodes path's "?" suffix. A missing or non-matching Content-Type comes back nil.

A file upload is get_multipart_params. It checks Content-Type for multipart/form-data and a boundary parameter, then splits request_body on it into a Map: a plain field's value is its content as a String, a file field's (one with a filename) is a Map of filename/content_type/content instead. A missing or non-multipart Content-Type, or one with no boundary, comes back nil; a part with no name is skipped rather than raising, the body being, like a JSON one, arbitrary text from outside the program.

params is request_body already parsed, eagerly, by new — unlike every get_*_params above, which parse lazily and hand back nil for the "wrong" Content-Type. new looks at Content-Type once: a .../json body is Json.parsed (kept only if it parses to a Map — a JSON array has no field names to key params by); an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body is decoded the same way get_form_params decodes it. Anything else — a multipart/form-data upload included, since that one is read lazily on purpose (see its own doc) — leaves params at {}, never nil, so a handler can Map.get(request.params, "id", nil) without checking first.

Both params and every get_*_params above understand bracket notation — application/x-www-form-urlencoded and query-string keys written name[] or name[key], the shape an HTML <form> and <a href="?..."> both write for a field meant to repeat or nest:

request =
  HttpRequest.new(
    "POST /items HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded\r\n\r\nids[]=1&ids[]=2&ids[]=3"
  )
request.params   # == {"ids": ["1", "2", "3"]}
request =
  HttpRequest.new(
    "POST /users HTTP/1.1\r\nContent-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded\r\n\r\nuser[name]=Alice&user[email]=alice%40example.com"
  )
request.params   # == {"user": {"name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com"}}

A bare name (no brackets) is unaffected — still the flat, last-value- wins Map entry it always was. name[] always appends a fresh element rather than looking for one to extend, which is what turns a repeated a[][b]=x&a[][c]=y into two elements, [{b: "x"}, {c: "y"}], instead of merging them into one; name[key] looks up (or starts) a nested Map at key and keeps going from there, so segments may nest to any depth (a[b][c]=x is {a: {b: {c: "x"}}}) and mix freely with [] at any position.

Functions

function new(text) Parses text into an HttpRequest: method, path, and version from the request line; headers as a List of (name, value) string tuples, in order, duplicates kept, names downcased; request_body, whatever follows the blank line ending the headers ("" if there is none); and params — request_body already parsed by Content-Type, {} when it names neither JSON nor a form (see the module doc for both, params and the bracket notation name[]/name[key] keys understand).
function get_method(self) self.method, the request line's verb ("GET", "POST", ...).
function get_path(self) self.path, the request line's target — whatever the client sent between the method and the version, query string and all (new does not parse it further; see String.split(path, "?") for that).
function get_http_version(self) self.version, the request line's HTTP version ("HTTP/1.1", ...).
function get_headers(self) self.headers, as a List of (name, value) string tuples, in order, duplicates kept, names downcased — see the module doc for why this is a List and not a Map.
function get_header(self, name) The value of the first header named name, matched case-insensitively — HTTP header names are case-insensitive by spec, which is also why every name in get_headers already comes back downcased; name is downcased the same way before it is compared. nil if there is no such header. Only the first match comes back; a header repeated on purpose (Set-Cookie, most commonly) needs get_headers and a filter to see every occurrence.
function get_request_body(self) self.request_body, whatever followed the blank line ending the headers ("" if there was none) — see the module doc for what a missing body versus an empty one each mean.
function get_cookies(self) The request's cookies, parsed out of its Cookie header (matched case-insensitively, like every HTTP header name) into a List of (name, value) string tuples — the Cookie-specific counterpart to get_headers, since a cookie header packs several name=value pairs into one ;-separated line that nothing else here unpacks.
function get_query_params(self) The request's query-string parameters, parsed out of self.path's "?" suffix into a Map — unlike headers/get_cookies, a repeated key has no protocol meaning to preserve, so the last occurrence simply wins, the same rule Map.put already uses for any other duplicate key. Parsed fresh on every call, straight from self.path — there is nowhere on an immutable HttpRequest to cache it, so new does no work for a request that never reads its query string.
function get_query_param(self, name) The value of the query-string parameter name, or nil if there is none — Map.get over get_query_params(), matched case-sensitively (unlike get_header, a query key has no HTTP-mandated case-insensitivity to honor).
function get_json_params(self) request_body parsed as JSON, but only when Content-Type says the body actually is JSON — a media type whose subtype is json (application/json, text/json, ...; matched case-insensitively, like every header, and read up to any ; a parameter such as charset starts). No Content-Type header, a media type that is not .../json, or a body that does not parse all come back nil — the same "just tell me you couldn't" contract Json.parse itself uses, so a handler never needs to check the header and the body's validity separately.
function get_form_params(self) request_body parsed as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, but only when Content-Type says so — the same decoding get_query_params uses on path's "?" suffix (+ to a space, %XX to the byte it names), since it is the same encoding, just carried in the body instead of the URL. A missing or non-application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Type comes back nil — the same contract get_json_params/ get_multipart_params use.
function get_multipart_params(self) request_body parsed as multipart/form-data, but only when Content-Type says so and carries a boundary — the delimiter that separates one part from the next, sent as Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=<boundary>. Each part is its own little header/body pair, Content-Disposition: form-data; name="..." naming the field it goes under: a plain field's value is its content as a String; a file field (one whose Content-Disposition also carries a filename) comes back as a Map of filename/content_type/content instead, content_type nil if the part sent none.

request_body parsed as multipart/form-data, but only when Content-Type says so and carries a boundary — the delimiter that separates one part from the next, sent as Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=<boundary>. A part with no name (no Content-Disposition at all, or one missing name) is skipped rather than raising, since request_body is arbitrary text from outside the program, same as a JSON one.

HttpResponse.title: HttpResponse — Ramos
HttpResponse.heading: HttpResponse
HttpResponse.body:
Summary

HttpResponse — the writable half of an HTTP response: a status, a List of (name, value) headers, and the Socket to write them (and the body) to. The natural companion to HttpRequest on the way out, and to HttpServer, whose handler receives the raw connection directly rather than returning response text (see that module's own doc):

Module documentation

HttpResponse — the writable half of an HTTP response: a status, a List of (name, value) headers, and the Socket to write them (and the body) to. The natural companion to HttpRequest on the way out, and to HttpServer, whose handler receives the raw connection directly rather than returning response text (see that module's own doc):

handler =
  do request, socket
    body = "hi"
    HttpResponse.new(socket)
    | HttpResponse.put_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
    | HttpResponse.put_header("Content-Length", "#{String.length(body)}")
    | HttpResponse.send_chunk(body)
HttpServer{port: 8080}.start(handler)

new opens with status: 200 and no headers — set both, then write:

response =
  HttpResponse.new(socket)
  | HttpResponse.set_status(404)
  | HttpResponse.put_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")

Like every other struct here, an instance is immutable — set_status, put_header, send_headers, and send_chunk all return a new HttpResponse rather than changing the one they were called on, the same self | Struct.put(...) convention Account.deposit uses in the guide. What is mutable is the connection itself: the struct only remembers whether the status line and headers have gone out yet (headers_sent), never any of the bytes already written — there is nowhere on an immutable value to buffer them, and Socket has no "peek what I already sent" to check instead.

Headers go out exactly once, on the first write. send_headers writes the status line and every header accumulated so far, then the blank line that ends them; send_chunk calls it first when it hasn't run yet, so a handler that never calls send_headers explicitly still gets a well-formed response the moment it writes its first chunk. Calling send_headers again afterward — directly, or through a further send_chunk — is a no-op: headers already on the wire can't be un-sent, so put_header/set_status after that point stop affecting what the client sees.

"In chunks" means repeated Socket.send calls, not HTTP's chunked Transfer-Encoding. HttpServer never keeps a connection open past one request (see its own doc), so a response can simply run until the socket closes — the same signal HTTP/1.0 always used for "body ends here" — with no Content-Length and no chunk-length framing required. A handler that wants a Content-Length-bearing response instead sets one with put_header before its first send_chunk, same as it always could when it built the whole response text by hand.

close is a convenience, not a requirement. HttpServer closes the connection itself once the handler returns (see its own doc), and Socket.close is idempotent, so calling it here too is harmless. Its only job is making sure headers go out even for a response whose handler never writes a body at all (a bare 204, say).

Functions

function new(socket) Builds an HttpResponse over socket: status: 200, no headers, nothing written yet.
function set_status(self, status) A new HttpResponse with status replaced. Has no effect on what the client sees once headers are already sent — see the module doc.
function put_header(self, name, value) A new HttpResponse with (name, value) appended to headers. Like HttpRequest.headers, this is a List, not a Map — a repeated put_header call (Set-Cookie, most commonly) keeps every occurrence rather than overwriting the last. Has no effect on what the client sees once headers are already sent — see the module doc.
function send_headers(self) Writes the status line and every accumulated header, then the blank line that ends them — "HTTP/1.1 <status> <reason>\r\n", one "<name>: <value>\r\n" per header, then "\r\n". A no-op, not a second write, when headers already went out (via an earlier send_headers or send_chunk).
function send_chunk(self, data) Writes one piece of the body, sending the status line and headers first when send_headers hasn't run yet. Call it as many times as there are pieces — each call is its own Socket.send, so the client sees data the moment this returns rather than once the whole response is built (see the module doc for what "in chunks" means here).
function close(self) Sends headers first when they haven't gone out yet — so a response with no body still reaches the client as valid HTTP — then closes the connection. HttpServer already closes the connection once the handler returns (see its own doc), so this is only needed to guarantee headers for a body-less response, or to close early from inside the handler itself.

Actor.title: Actor — Ramos
Actor.heading: Actor
Actor.body:
Summary

Actor — a named process that holds state and answers messages.

Module documentation

Actor — a named process that holds state and answers messages.

A module implements Actor by defining one function, call, which takes the operation, its arguments, the actor's current state and its config, and returns a (reply, new_state) tuple. The actor's state is whatever the last call returned; nothing mutates, the actor simply holds the newest value.

module Counter
  implements Actor
function call(f, args, state, config)
  case f
    :bump -> (state + 1, state + 1)
    :read -> (state, state)
function start()
  start_actor(:counter, Counter, 0, {})
function bump()
  call_actor(:counter, Counter, :bump, [])

The convention is to keep call as the server half and wrap each operation in a plain function — the client half — so callers never write call_actor themselves.

Each actor runs on its own thread, with its own memory: a fresh scope that cannot see the caller's bindings, and state reachable only by sending a message. One actor handles its own messages one at a time, in order, but different actors run in parallel.

That memory does not include the actor registry, so a handler cannot send messages to another actor or to itself.

Functions

function cast(f, args, state, config) Handle one message sent with cast_actor, returning only the new state — a cast has no reply to send anywhere, which is the whole difference from call.
function call(f, args, state, config) Handle one message. Required — every implementer defines it.

The default runs the module's own call and discards the reply, so an actor that already handles an operation synchronously can be cast to without writing anything extra. Override it for work that only makes sense fire-and-forget.

cast_actor returns as soon as the message is sent, so the handler may still be running when the next statement starts.

Global.title: Global — Ramos
Global.heading: Global
Global.body:
Summary

Global — one process-wide map, held by an actor.

Module documentation

Global — one process-wide map, held by an actor.

Global is a Map that every part of a program shares: one actor named :global holds it, and get / put / clear are messages to that actor. Nothing mutates — each put hands the actor a new map, and the actor keeps the newest one.

Global.start()
Global.put(:user, "andrew")
Global.get(:user)             # == "andrew"

Only get waits. A write has no answer worth waiting for, so put and clear are casts: :ok comes back as soon as the message is sent. That costs nothing in correctness, because the actor takes its mailbox in order — a get sent after a put is handled after it, and sees the write.

Use it with caution. It is shared mutable state wearing an actor's clothes, and it carries every cost that implies:

  • It hides a dependency. A function that reads Global says nothing about it in its signature, so callers cannot see what it needs or substitute anything for a test. A parameter is almost always better.
  • It is a bottleneck. One actor handles one message at a time, so every reader and writer in the program queues behind the same thread.
  • It has no scoping. One flat key space for the whole program, so two unrelated parts picking the same key silently overwrite each other.
  • A read is a guess. Between a get and the put that acts on it, another caller may have written the key; only what happens inside one handler is atomic.
  • Actors cannot reach it. An actor's thread cannot see the actor registry, so a handler cannot call Global.get — a message is the only way state gets into an actor.

Reach for it for what is genuinely process-wide and written once: config read at startup, a feature flag, a run id. For anything else, pass the value or give it its own actor with a name that says what it holds.

Global is an ordinary Actor implementation, so list_actors, actor_stats(:global) and stop_actor(:global) all work on it.

Functions

function get(key) The value stored under key, waiting for the actor to answer. Every write sent before it has been handled by the time it reads.
function put(key, value) Store value under key, replacing whatever was there, without waiting for the actor. :ok comes back at once and the next get still sees the write, because the actor handles its messages in order.
function clear(key) Drop key without waiting for the actor, on the same terms as put. Clearing a key that is not there is fine.

Pool.title: Pool — Ramos
Pool.heading: Pool
Pool.body:
Summary

Pool — a fixed-size pool of some resource, held by an actor, generalizing Global's "one actor, one shared value" to "one actor per named pool, many resources."

Module documentation

Pool — a fixed-size pool of some resource, held by an actor, generalizing Global's "one actor, one shared value" to "one actor per named pool, many resources."

new starts a pool under an id you choose — like start_actor, the id is what tells one pool from another, so a program can run several. Its config says how to grow the pool: min resources are built right away, factory (a lambda of no arguments) builds one more whenever checkin needs one and the pool is under max.

config = {min: 2, max: 5, factory: do -> Socket.connect("db.internal", 5432)}
(:ok, id) = Pool.new(:db_pool, config)
(:ok, (ref, conn)) = Pool.checkin(id)   # hand out a connection
# ... use conn ...
Pool.checkout(id, ref)                  # give it back

Naming reads like a hotel, not like most connection-pool libraries. checkin is the one that hands you a resource — like checking into a room, you are the one using it now — and checkout is the one that gives it back — like checking out, freeing the room for the next guest. Libraries such as Ruby's ConnectionPool or Erlang's poolboy use the opposite pairing (checkout to acquire). If you know one of those, read checkin/checkout here backwards from what you'd expect.

Every resource the pool hands out is tracked by a ref — an integer checkin returns alongside the resource — because two resources are not necessarily distinguishable any other way: a Socket or Thread handle has no structural identity (== on two of them is always false, even against itself), so the pool cannot find "the same one" back by comparing values. checkout always takes the ref checkin gave you.

A resource is never validated, health-checked, or closed by Pool itself — it has no idea what a Socket or a Thread even is, only that factory() builds one and that it is a plain value from then on. Closing or resetting whatever came out of checkin before treating it as good again is on the caller.

checkin/checkout cannot be called from inside a Thread.started lambda, or from inside another actor's handler. This is not a Pool limitation specifically — it is the same rule every actor lives under (see Thread's and Actor's own docs): a spawned thread gets a fresh, empty actor registry and "cannot see the caller's running actors," and a handler is isolated the same way. In practice: a pool has to be checked in and out from your program's own top-level flow (or plain functions it calls directly) — never from a per-connection Thread.start, and never from inside another actor. Naming a pool after a use that sounds thread-per-something (a thread pool, a connection pool drawn from inside concurrent handlers) is the trap this warns about: Pool itself is not reachable from there.

A factory that raises is not a soft failure. There is no try/catch in Ramos, so unlike :pool_exhausted — a proper (:error, ...) value checkin returns — a runtime error inside factory crashes whatever called checkin, not just that one call. The pool's own actor is unaffected and keeps running (an actor survives an error in one message and moves on to the next, same as any actor), but nothing in the caller can see that from the inside — from where checkin was called, this looks exactly like any other uncaught error. Keep factory itself free of anything that can raise, or guard what it does before handing it to Pool.new.

Pool is an ordinary Actor implementation, so list_actors, actor_stats(id) and stop_actor(id) all work on any pool it starts — stop_actor does not close what the pool was holding, for the same reason Pool never does.

Config.title: Config — Ramos
Config.heading: Config
Config.body:
Summary

Config — the environment's .env file, read once and answered from memory.

Module documentation

Config — the environment's .env file, read once and answered from memory.

One actor named :config holds the settings for this run. start picks the file from the APP_ENV environment variable, reads it, parses it, and hands the result to the actor; from then on get is the only operation. Nothing writes — the actor is read-only, so what a program sees at the end of a run is what it saw at the start.

The examples here and below are written against this .env.dev — dev is where APP_ENV defaults to, so this is the file an unset environment (as here) reads:

# ramos doctest setup
settings =
  """
    [database]
    host = "db.internal"
    port = 5432
  """
File.write(".env.dev", settings)

Read back, that is:

Config.start()                   # == :ok
Config.get("database", "host")   # == "db.internal"
Config.get("database", "port")   # == "5432"
Config.get("database", "user")   # == nil

Which file. APP_ENV names the environment and the file is .env followed by its downcased name — APP_ENV=PROD reads .env.prod, APP_ENV=staging reads .env.staging. Unset or empty, that downcased name defaults to dev, so a project reads .env.dev — and so runs — without anything set. path() reports the choice without starting anything. The path is relative, so it resolves against the working directory the program was run from.

The format is TOML, of the subset a settings file actually uses: [section] headers, key = value pairs, # comments, blank lines. Every value comes back as a String — port = 5432 reads as "5432" — because the file cannot say what a value was meant to be and guessing would make get return a different type for the same key on a different deploy. Use to_integer on the way out when you need a number.

Quotes around a value are stripped, single or double. An unquoted value ends at a trailing # comment; a quoted one does not, so a # inside quotes is part of the value. A key that appears twice takes its last value, and a key written before the first [section] has no section to be asked for, so it is skipped.

Missing files are not an error to get. start reports an unreadable file with error — (:error, (:config_file_not_found, message, _)) when no file matches APP_ENV, (:error, (reason, message, _)) in File's own vocabulary for anything else — so the caller decides whether a run without config is fatal:

case Config.start()
  :ok -> run()
  (:error, (:config_file_not_found, _, _)) -> run_with_defaults()

Config is an ordinary Actor implementation, so list_actors, actor_stats(:config) and stop_actor(:config) all work on it. For state that changes as a program runs, see Global.

Functions

function call(f, args, state, config) The server half. :get is the only operation — the settings are fixed for the run, so there is nothing else to ask for.
function start() Read the environment's file and start the :config actor on it. Call it once, before anything reads; starting it twice is an error.
function get(section, key) The value of key under [section], as a String.
function path() The file start will read: .env.<downcased APP_ENV>, or .env.dev when it is unset or empty — dev is the default environment. Reads nothing itself.
helper env_name()
helper path_for(env)
helper not_found_message()
helper get_impl(args, state)
helper parse(text)
helper parse_line(acc, raw)
helper is_skippable(line)
helper is_header(line)
helper header_name(line)
helper put_pair(sections, section, line)
helper put_entry(sections, section, key, value)
helper key_of(line, split)
helper value_of(line, split)
helper unquote(value)
helper take_quoted(value, quote)
helper drop_comment(value)

function call(f, args, state, config) ¶

The server half. :get is the only operation — the settings are fixed for the run, so there is nothing else to ask for.

f
the operation — :get
args
[section, key], the pair to look up
state

config

Returns: a (value, state) tuple; a read leaves the settings alone

function start() ¶

Read the environment's file and start the :config actor on it. Call it once, before anything reads; starting it twice is an error.

Reading happens here rather than inside the actor, so a missing or unreadable file surfaces at the call that started it.

read: `(:config_file_not_found, message, stacktrace)` names the
environment and the path when no file matches `APP_ENV`; any other
reason — a permissions error, say — passes through in `File`'s own
vocabulary, `(reason, message, stacktrace)`
Config.start()   # == :ok
Config.get("database", "host")   # == "db.internal"

function get(section, key) ¶

The value of key under [section], as a String.

not in the file
Config.start()
Config.get("database", "host")   # == "db.internal"

Config.get("nope", "host")       # == nil

key

Returns: the value as a String, or nil when the section or the key is

The file start will read: .env.<downcased APP_ENV>, or .env.dev when it is unset or empty — dev is the default environment. Reads nothing itself.

With APP_ENV=PROD this reads .env.prod; unset, as here, it is .env.dev:

Config.path()   # == ".env.dev"

Thread.title: Thread — Ramos
Thread.heading: Thread
Thread.body:
Summary

Thread — run a computation on another thread and collect its result.

Module documentation

Thread — run a computation on another thread and collect its result.

A thread is a one-shot piece of parallel work. start starts a zero-argument lambda on its own thread and hands back a handle at once, without waiting; await waits on the handle and returns what the lambda produced. Between the two, the caller and the spawned work run at the same time.

t = Thread.start(do -> slow_sum())
other_work()                        # runs while the thread does
total = Thread.await(t)             # now wait for it

To fan several out and gather them, start them all, then await_all the handles — every thread is already running, so the wait is for the slowest, not the sum:

[do -> a(), do -> b(), do -> c()]
| List.map(do f -> Thread.start(f))
| Thread.await_all()

The concurrency is real. Two threads each sleeping 300ms finish in ~300ms, not 600 — the sleeps overlap.

A thread produces a value, where an [[Actor]] holds state and answers messages over its lifetime. Reach for a thread to fan a batch of independent work out and gather it back; reach for an actor for something long-lived that many callers talk to.

What crosses to the worker is the lambda alone — it carries its own captured scope. Everything else is fresh, exactly as for an actor: the worker has its own root and cannot see the caller's running actors, so a started lambda cannot message an actor. A failure inside the lambda is not lost; it surfaces as a runtime error at the await that collects it.

A thread's output is live: it prints to the same place as the caller, as it happens, so a started println may land in either order relative to the caller's — though never split, since a whole line is written at once. (An actor is the opposite: it buffers and delivers its output at the reply, so actor lines never interleave.)

Await what you start. A handle is a value, so it can be held, passed, and awaited from anywhere — but a thread nobody awaits is detached: its result is never collected, and it may be cut off when the program ends. There is no registry of threads and no automatic wait at program end; the handle is the only way back to the work.

Functions

function start(f) Starts f, a lambda of no arguments, on its own thread and returns a handle at once — the caller does not wait. Pass the handle to await for the result.
function await(t) Waits for the thread t to finish and returns what its lambda produced. A failure inside the lambda comes back here as a runtime error. The thread's output is written now, once; awaiting the same handle again returns the same value without printing twice.
function await_all(threads) Waits for every thread in threads and returns their results as a list, in the same order as the handles — however the threads happened to finish. Since each was already running, this waits for the slowest, not the sum.
function map(list, f) A parallel List.map: f is applied to every element on its own thread, and the results are gathered in order. Every element's work overlaps, so a list of slow, independent computations finishes in about the time of the slowest rather than their sum.
function each(list, f) Like map, but for side effects: f runs on its own thread for every element, all of them are waited for, and nil comes back. Use it to run a batch of independent effects at once and be sure they have all finished.

function start(f) ¶

Starts f, a lambda of no arguments, on its own thread and returns a handle at once — the caller does not wait. Pass the handle to await for the result.

Has no Ramos body beyond the native call: starting a thread runs a lambda, which an ordinary native handler cannot do — reaching back into the evaluator to run it — so the interpreter intercepts this particular native call rather than dispatching it through the plain native table.

t = Thread.start(do -> 6 * 7)
Thread.await(t)   # == 42
f
a lambda of no arguments

Returns: a Thread handle

function await(t) ¶

Waits for the thread t to finish and returns what its lambda produced. A failure inside the lambda comes back here as a runtime error. The thread's output is written now, once; awaiting the same handle again returns the same value without printing twice.

Has no Ramos body beyond the native call, for the reason given on start.

Thread.await(Thread.start(do -> "done"))   # == "done"
t
a Thread handle from start

Returns: whatever the started lambda returned

function await_all(threads) ¶

Waits for every thread in threads and returns their results as a list, in the same order as the handles — however the threads happened to finish. Since each was already running, this waits for the slowest, not the sum.

A failure in any of them surfaces as a runtime error, from the first handle whose thread failed. Pair it with start to run a batch at once:

[do -> 1 + 1, do -> 2 + 2]
| List.map(do f -> Thread.start(f))
| Thread.await_all()                # == [2, 4]
Thread.await_all([Thread.start(do -> :a), Thread.start(do -> :b)])   # == [:a, :b]
threads
a List of Thread handles from start

Returns: a List of their results, in the order of the handles

function map(list, f) ¶

A parallel List.map: f is applied to every element on its own thread, and the results are gathered in order. Every element's work overlaps, so a list of slow, independent computations finishes in about the time of the slowest rather than their sum.

f runs on another thread, so it cannot reach the caller's actors — the same rule as start. Order is preserved: the result lines up with list however the threads happen to finish.

Thread.map([1, 2, 3], do n -> n * n)   # == [1, 4, 9]
list
the list to map over
f
a lambda applied to each element, on its own thread

Returns: a new list of f applied to each element, in the original order

function each(list, f) ¶

Like map, but for side effects: f runs on its own thread for every element, all of them are waited for, and nil comes back. Use it to run a batch of independent effects at once and be sure they have all finished.

Thread.each([1, 2, 3], do n -> n)   # == nil
list
the list to iterate over
f
a lambda run once per element, on its own thread, for its effect

Returns: nil

Test.title: Test — Ramos
Test.heading: Test
Test.body:
Summary

Test — the trait that marks a module as a test module.

Module documentation

Test — the trait that marks a module as a test module.

A test module is an ordinary module that implements Test. Every public function whose name begins with test_ is a test, and ramos test runs them. Nothing registers itself and there is no test DSL: a test is a function, and a failing assert is what makes it fail.

# src/test/my_app/user_test.rmo
module MyApp.UserTest
  implements Test
alias MyApp.User
function test_user_hello()
  user = User{name: "Andrew"}
  assert(user.hello() == "Ola Andrew")

Tests live under src/test/, and follow the same rules as any other file: the namespace is the path, so MyApp.UserTest is src/test/my_app/user_test.rmo. A test module's name must end in Test, which is what makes it read as one in a failure report. A test reaches the code it exercises through the ordinary alias, resolved against src/.

ramos test with no argument runs everything under src/test/; with a file argument it runs just that file.

The trait requires nothing — it is a marker, so being run is something a module opts into rather than something its name causes. A test module may define helpers alongside its tests; only public test_ functions are called, and each is called with no arguments.

A test stops at its first failed assert, and the run continues with the next test. See Kernel.assert for what a failure reports.

Module.title: Module — Ramos
Module.heading: Module
Module.body:
Summary

Module — introspecting and calling into modules by value.

Module documentation

Module — introspecting and calling into modules by value.

A module is itself a value in Ramos: Kernel (or Integer, or any module written) can be bound, passed around, and stored — is_module tests for one and type_of names it. This module is what you do with one once you have it, when the function to call is not known at the call site.

# ramos doctest setup
module Greeter
  function hello(name)
    "hi #{name}"
helper secret()
  42
Module.functions(Greeter)                    # == ["hello"]
Module.apply(Greeter, "hello", ["Andrew"])    # == "hi Andrew"

Conventions:

  • both functions only ever see a module's public functions — helper stays exactly as unreachable from here as it is from a written Greeter.secret() call outside the module.
  • a function is named with a String ("hello"), not a Symbol — matching type_of, since a module's own name is a String too.

Functions

function functions(m) The names of the public functions m defines, in declaration order. helper functions are never included — they are not callable from outside m either.
function apply(m, fn_name, args) Resolves fn_name on module m and calls it with args, a list of its arguments — like Kernel.apply, but the function is looked up by name on a module rather than held as a lambda. Use it when which function to call is only known at runtime (a dispatch table, a plugin name read from config); otherwise call the function directly.

function functions(m) ¶

The names of the public functions m defines, in declaration order. helper functions are never included — they are not callable from outside m either.

Module.functions(Greeter)   # == ["hello"]
m
the module to inspect

Returns: a List of String function names, in declaration order

function apply(m, fn_name, args) ¶

Resolves fn_name on module m and calls it with args, a list of its arguments — like Kernel.apply, but the function is looked up by name on a module rather than held as a lambda. Use it when which function to call is only known at runtime (a dispatch table, a plugin name read from config); otherwise call the function directly.

Has no Ramos body: the interpreter intercepts the call, because resolving fn_name and running it needs the evaluator, which a native cannot reach. Raises if m has no public function named fn_name.

Module.apply(Integer, "abs", [-7])   # == 7
m
the module to call a function on
fn_name
the function's name, as a String
args
a List of the arguments to pass

Returns: whatever the resolved function returns

examples.title: Examples — Ramos
examples.body:
Examples

One short program per language feature, each taken straight from the fixtures in tests/fixtures/features/ — so every snippet here lexes and parses as real Ramos.

For the prose version of the same ground, see the language guide.

  • Actor a module implements Actor by defining call, which returns (reply, new_state). cast has no reply: it returns only the new state, and runs later — before the next call, or at program end.
  • Alias alias gives a module a shorter name, cutting the verbosity of long namespaces. It works for pure modules and struct modules alike.
